units.title: TEST POSITIONING
units.summary: The subject can either sit or stand.
summary_sentences: The subject can either sit or stand.

units.title: ACTION
units.summary: The examiner taps over the masseter muscle and parotid gland (Figure 1-1).
summary_sentences: The examiner taps over the masseter muscle and parotid gland (Figure 1-1).

units.title: POSITIVE FINDING
units.summary: Twitching of the facial muscles, especially the masseter, indicates positive findings for facial nerve pathology.
summary_sentences: Twitching of the facial muscles, especially the masseter, indicates positive findings for facial nerve pathology.

units.title: SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS/COMMENTS
units.summary: Twitching of the facial muscles may also be a result of low calcium levels in the blood. A positive finding of this nature has also been referred to as a Weiss sign.
summary_sentences: Twitching of the facial muscles may also be a result of low calcium levels in the blood.
A positive finding of this nature has also been referred to as a Weiss sign.

units.title: TEST POSITIONING
units.summary: The subject sits upright in a chair.
summary_sentences: The subject sits upright in a chair.

units.title: ACTION
units.summary: The examiner places a cotton roll between the molars on the unin-volved side and instructs the subject to bite down forcefully.
summary_sentences: The examiner places a cotton roll between the molars on the unin-volved side and instructs the subject to bite down forcefully.

units.title: POSITIVE FINDING
units.summary: The reporting of pain on the involved side by the subject indicates a positive finding, which may be reflective of an anteriorly dislocated disk.
summary_sentences: The reporting of pain on the involved side by the subject indicates a positive finding, which may be reflective of an anteriorly dislocated disk.

units.title: SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS/COMMENTS
units.summary: The subject may be instructed to chew on the cotton, as opposed to forcefully biting down. A positive finding for pain may suggest any number of temporomandibular pathologies.
summary_sentences: The subject may be instructed to chew on the cotton, as opposed to forcefully biting down.
A positive finding for pain may suggest any number of temporomandibular pathologies.

units.title: TEST POSITIONING
units.summary: The subject sits upright in a chair.
summary_sentences: The subject sits upright in a chair.

units.title: ACTION
units.summary: The examiner faces the subject and places his fifth digits in the sub-ject's ears. The subject is instructed to repeatedly open and close the mouth while the examiner applies pressure in an anterior direction using the pads of the fifth digits (Figures 1-2A and 1-2B).
summary_sentences: The examiner faces the subject and places his fifth digits in the sub-ject's ears.
The subject is instructed to repeatedly open and close the mouth while the examiner applies pressure in an anterior direction using the pads of the fifth digits (Figures 1-2A and 1-2B).

units.title: POSITIVE FINDING
units.summary: The subject's reporting of pain or discomfort during opening and closing of the mouth when pressure is applied indicates a positive test. This may be a result of inflammation to the synovium of the temporo-mandibular joint (TMJ).
summary_sentences: The subject's reporting of pain or discomfort during opening and closing of the mouth when pressure is applied indicates a positive test.
This may be a result of inflammation to the synovium of the temporo-mandibular joint (TMJ).

units.summary: The subjective reporting of pain can be a result of any pathology to

units.title: TEST POSITIONING
units.summary: The subject lies supine, and the examiner sits with both hands sup-porting the subject's head.
summary_sentences: The subject lies supine, and the examiner sits with both hands sup-porting the subject's head.

units.title: ACTION
units.summary: Slowly extend, rotate, and laterally flex the subject's cervical spine to each side. Then observe the subject for dizziness, blurred vision, nys-tagmus, slurred speech, or loss of consciousness (Figure 2-1). Each posi-tion should be held for approximately 30 seconds.
summary_sentences: Slowly extend, rotate, and laterally flex the subject's cervical spine to each side.
Then observe the subject for dizziness, blurred vision, nys-tagmus, slurred speech, or loss of consciousness (Figure 2-1).
Each posi-tion should be held for approximately 30 seconds.

units.title: POSITIVE FINDING
units.summary: Dizziness, blurred vision, nystagmus, slurred speech, or loss of con-sciousness are indicative of partial or complete occlusion of the verte-bral artery.
summary_sentences: Dizziness, blurred vision, nystagmus, slurred speech, or loss of con-sciousness are indicative of partial or complete occlusion of the verte-bral artery.

units.title: SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS/COMMENTS
units.summary: The aforementioned signs and symptoms should be considered con-traindications for such treatments as traction and joint mobilizations.
summary_sentences: The aforementioned signs and symptoms should be considered con-traindications for such treatments as traction and joint mobilizations.

units.title: TEST POSITIONING
units.summary: With the subject seated comfortably, the examiner rests the volar surface of both hands on top of the subject's head (Figure 2-2A).
summary_sentences: With the subject seated comfortably, the examiner rests the volar surface of both hands on top of the subject's head (Figure 2-2A).

units.title: ACTION
units.summary: The examiner applies a downward pressure while the subject lateral-ly flexes the head. The test is repeated with the subject laterally flexing to the opposite side. Lateral flexion may be performed both actively and passively (Figure 2-2B).
summary_sentences: The examiner applies a downward pressure while the subject lateral-ly flexes the head.
The test is repeated with the subject laterally flexing to the opposite side.
Lateral flexion may be performed both actively and passively (Figure 2-2B).

units.title: POSITIVE FINDING
units.summary: During the application of compression, a reporting of pain into the upper extremity toward the same side that the head is laterally flexed is positive. This indicates pressure on a nerve root, which can be correlat-ed by the dermatomal distribution of the pain.
summary_sentences: During the application of compression, a reporting of pain into the upper extremity toward the same side that the head is laterally flexed is positive.
This indicates pressure on a nerve root, which can be correlat-ed by the dermatomal distribution of the pain.

units.title: SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS/COMMENTS
units.summary: Precautions (and possibly avoidance) should be taken with compres-sion of the vertebral area with a subject who has been diagnosed with conditions such as osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, osteoporosis, and spinal stenosis. [he examiner should perform the vertebral artery test as a screen prior to administering this special test.
summary_sentences: Precautions (and possibly avoidance) should be taken with compres-sion of the vertebral area with a subject who has been diagnosed with conditions such as osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, osteoporosis, and spinal stenosis.
[he examiner should perform the vertebral artery test as a screen prior to administering this special test.

units.title: TEST POSITIONING
units.summary: With the subject seated, the examiner places one hand under the subject's chin and the other hand around the occiput (Figure 2-3).
summary_sentences: With the subject seated, the examiner places one hand under the subject's chin and the other hand around the occiput (Figure 2-3).

units.title: ACTION
units.summary: The examiner slowly distracts the subject's head from the trunk while the subject remains in a relaxed position.
summary_sentences: The examiner slowly distracts the subject's head from the trunk while the subject remains in a relaxed position.

units.title: POSITIVE FINDING
units.summary: The finding is positive when existing complaints of pain decrease or disappear during the distraction. This indicates that a nerve root com-pression may exist while the subject sustains normal posture and/or positioning.
summary_sentences: The finding is positive when existing complaints of pain decrease or disappear during the distraction.
This indicates that a nerve root com-pression may exist while the subject sustains normal posture and/or positioning.

units.title: SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS/COMMENTS
units.summary: Distraction of the cervical area for the assessment of a nerve root impingement should not be performed on a subject who has vertebral instability. Any increase in pain may indicate muscular and/or ligamen-tous damage. The examiner should perform the vertebral artery test as a screen prior to administering this special test.
summary_sentences: Distraction of the cervical area for the assessment of a nerve root impingement should not be performed on a subject who has vertebral instability.
Any increase in pain may indicate muscular and/or ligamen-tous damage.
The examiner should perform the vertebral artery test as a screen prior to administering this special test.

units.title: TEST POSITIONING
units.summary: The examiner stands next to the subject.
summary_sentences: The examiner stands next to the subject.

units.title: ACTION
units.summary: The examiner asks the subject to take a deep breath and hold while bearing down, as if having a bowel movement.
summary_sentences: The examiner asks the subject to take a deep breath and hold while bearing down, as if having a bowel movement.

units.title: POSITIVE FINDING
units.summary: Increased pain due to increased intrathecal pressure, which may be secondary to a space-occupying lesion, herniated disk, tumor, or osteo-phyte in the cervical canal is a positive finding. Pain may be localized or referred to the corresponding dermatome.
summary_sentences: Increased pain due to increased intrathecal pressure, which may be secondary to a space-occupying lesion, herniated disk, tumor, or osteo-phyte in the cervical canal is a positive finding.
Pain may be localized or referred to the corresponding dermatome.

units.title: SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS/COMMENTS
units.summary: The increased pressure may alter venous function and cause dizziness or unconsciousness. [he examiner should be prepared to steady the sub-fECt:

units.title: TEST POSITIONING
units.summary: The examiner stands next to the subject.
summary_sentences: The examiner stands next to the subject.

units.title: ACTION
units.summary: The examiner asks the subject to swallow.
summary_sentences: The examiner asks the subject to swallow.

units.title: POSITIVE FINDING
units.summary: Increased pain or difficulty swallowing (dysphagia) caused by anteri-or cervical spine obstructions, such as vertebral subluxations, osteo-phyte protrusion, soft tissue swelling, or tumors in the anterior cervical spine region, is positive.
summary_sentences: Increased pain or difficulty swallowing (dysphagia) caused by anteri-or cervical spine obstructions, such as vertebral subluxations, osteo-phyte protrusion, soft tissue swelling, or tumors in the anterior cervical spine region, is positive.

units.title: SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS/COMMENTS
units.summary: Be certain the subject's head is neutral, as swallowing becomes more difficult with the neck extended.
summary_sentences: Be certain the subject's head is neutral, as swallowing becomes more difficult with the neck extended.

units.title: TEST POSITIONING
units.summary: The subject can sit or lie supine.
summary_sentences: The subject can sit or lie supine.

units.title: ACTION
units.summary: The examiner gently taps the cervical area near Erb’s point. Erb's point can be found anterior to the transverse process of C6, approxi-mately 2 cm superior to the location of the clavicle (Figure 2-4).
summary_sentences: The examiner gently taps the cervical area near Erb’s point.
Erb's point can be found anterior to the transverse process of C6, approxi-mately 2 cm superior to the location of the clavicle (Figure 2-4).

units.title: POSITIVE FINDING
units.summary: A subjective reporting of a change in sensation to the upper extrem-ity on the ipsilateral side resulting in increased pain or absent/dimin-ished sensation is positive, indicating brachial plexus pathology.
summary_sentences: A subjective reporting of a change in sensation to the upper extrem-ity on the ipsilateral side resulting in increased pain or absent/dimin-ished sensation is positive, indicating brachial plexus pathology.

units.title: SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS/COMMENTS
units.summary: This area is believed to be where the proximal portion of the brachial plexus is most superficial. A positive finding should be combined with a complete cervical nerve root assessment prior to any involved patholo-gy to the brachial plexus.
summary_sentences: This area is believed to be where the proximal portion of the brachial plexus is most superficial.
A positive finding should be combined with a complete cervical nerve root assessment prior to any involved patholo-gy to the brachial plexus.

units.title: TEST POSITIONING
units.summary: The subject stands with both shoulders abducted to 90 degrees, hori-zontally adducted 30 degrees, and internally rotated so the subject's thumbs face the floor (Figure 3-1).
summary_sentences: The subject stands with both shoulders abducted to 90 degrees, hori-zontally adducted 30 degrees, and internally rotated so the subject's thumbs face the floor (Figure 3-1).

units.title: ACTION
units.summary: The examiner resists the subject's attempts to actively forward elevate both shoulders.
summary_sentences: The examiner resists the subject's attempts to actively forward elevate both shoulders.

units.title: POSITIVE FINDING
units.summary: Involvement of the supraspinatus muscle and/or tendon is suspected with noted weakness and/or a report of pain.
summary_sentences: Involvement of the supraspinatus muscle and/or tendon is suspected with noted weakness and/or a report of pain.

units.title: SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS/COMMENTS
units.summary: Weakness of the supraspinatus muscle may be a result of suprascapu-lar nerve involvement. Reported pain may be indicative of tendinitis and/or impingement.
summary_sentences: Weakness of the supraspinatus muscle may be a result of suprascapu-lar nerve involvement.
Reported pain may be indicative of tendinitis and/or impingement.

units.title: TEST POSITIONING
units.summary: The subject sits with the elbow flexed to 90 degrees and stabilized against the thorax. The forearm is in a pronated position. The examiner places one hand along the subject's forearm and the other hand on the proximal portion of the subject's humerus, near the bicipital groove (Figure 3-2A).
summary_sentences: The subject sits with the elbow flexed to 90 degrees and stabilized against the thorax.
The forearm is in a pronated position.
The examiner places one hand along the subject's forearm and the other hand on the proximal portion of the subject's humerus, near the bicipital groove (Figure 3-2A).

units.title: ACTION
units.summary: The examiner resists the subject's attempt to actively supinate the forearm and externally rotate the humerus (Figure 3-2B).
summary_sentences: The examiner resists the subject's attempt to actively supinate the forearm and externally rotate the humerus (Figure 3-2B).

units.title: POSITIVE FINDING
units.summary: Pain that is reported to exist in the area of the bicipital groove is a positive finding that may indicate bicipital tendinitis.
summary_sentences: Pain that is reported to exist in the area of the bicipital groove is a positive finding that may indicate bicipital tendinitis.

units.title: SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS/COMMENTS
units.summary: This is a difficult test to perform. One may be just as accurate to assess bicipital tendinitis by simply palpating the long head of the biceps ten-don in the bicipital groove.
summary_sentences: This is a difficult test to perform.
One may be just as accurate to assess bicipital tendinitis by simply palpating the long head of the biceps ten-don in the bicipital groove.

units.title: TEST POSITIONING
units.summary: The subject sits on a table or stands. The involved shoulder is flexed to 90 degrees, the elbow is fully extended, and the forearm is supinated. The examiner places one hand along the volar aspect of the subject's forearm and the other hand on the proximal aspect of the subject's humerus near the area of the bicipital groove (Figure 3-3).
summary_sentences: The subject sits on a table or stands.
The involved shoulder is flexed to 90 degrees, the elbow is fully extended, and the forearm is supinated.
The examiner places one hand along the volar aspect of the subject's forearm and the other hand on the proximal aspect of the subject's humerus near the area of the bicipital groove (Figure 3-3).

units.title: ACTION
units.summary: The examiner resists the subject's attempt to actively flex the humerus forward.
summary_sentences: The examiner resists the subject's attempt to actively flex the humerus forward.

units.title: POSITIVE FINDING
units.summary: Tenderness and/or pain in the bicipital groove is a positive finding that may suggest bicipital tendinitis.
summary_sentences: Tenderness and/or pain in the bicipital groove is a positive finding that may suggest bicipital tendinitis.

units.title: SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS/COMMENTS
units.summary: The examiner should carefully watch that the forearm is supinated and that the subject does not use accessory muscles to mask any exist-ing weakness.
summary_sentences: The examiner should carefully watch that the forearm is supinated and that the subject does not use accessory muscles to mask any exist-ing weakness.

units.title: TEST POSITIONING
units.summary: The subject sits or stands while the examiner stands directly behind the subject. The subject interlocks his fingers and places them on the superior/posterior aspect of his head.
summary_sentences: The subject sits or stands while the examiner stands directly behind the subject.
The subject interlocks his fingers and places them on the superior/posterior aspect of his head.

units.title: ACTION
units.summary: The examiner palpates the long head of the biceps tendon bilateral-ly while the subject contracts both the left and right biceps brachii mus-cles simultaneously (Figure 3-4). PosiTivVE FINDING Increased pain is indicative of a biceps brachii long head tendinitis. Decreased tension of the tendon with palpation may indicate an inabil-ity or apprehension of the biceps brachii to contract forcefully.
summary_sentences: The examiner palpates the long head of the biceps tendon bilateral-ly while the subject contracts both the left and right biceps brachii mus-cles simultaneously (Figure 3-4).
PosiTivVE FINDING Increased pain is indicative of a biceps brachii long head tendinitis.
Decreased tension of the tendon with palpation may indicate an inabil-ity or apprehension of the biceps brachii to contract forcefully.

units.title: SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS/COMMENTS
units.summary: The subject should be sure to stabilize the humeral head during the contraction and allow for the hands to push into the stabilized humeral head. No tension may be the result of a biceps brachii long head rupture. Rupture of the long head of the biceps flexor cubiti muscle.
summary_sentences: The subject should be sure to stabilize the humeral head during the contraction and allow for the hands to push into the stabilized humeral head.
No tension may be the result of a biceps brachii long head rupture.
Rupture of the long head of the biceps flexor cubiti muscle.

units.title: TEST POSITIONING
units.summary: The subject sits on a table or stands.
summary_sentences: The subject sits on a table or stands.

units.title: ACTION
units.summary: The examiner passively abducts the subject's involved arm to 90 degrees and then instructs the subject to slowly lower the arm to the side (Figures 3-5A and 3-5B).
summary_sentences: The examiner passively abducts the subject's involved arm to 90 degrees and then instructs the subject to slowly lower the arm to the side (Figures 3-5A and 3-5B).

units.title: POSITIVE FINDING
units.summary: The subject is unable to slowly return the arm to the side and/or has significant pain when attempting to perform the task. This is indicative of rotator cuff pathology.
summary_sentences: The subject is unable to slowly return the arm to the side and/or has significant pain when attempting to perform the task.
This is indicative of rotator cuff pathology.

units.title: SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS/COMMENTS
units.summary: If the examiner suspects rotator cuff pathology prior to performing the test, he should prepare to rapidly assist the subject in the event that the subject does experience an inability to control the adduction move-ment of the arm. REFERENCE Calis M, Akgun K, Birtane M, Karacan I,Calis H, Tuzun F. Diagnostic values of clinical diagnostic tests in subacromial impingement syndrome.
summary_sentences: If the examiner suspects rotator cuff pathology prior to performing the test, he should prepare to rapidly assist the subject in the event that the subject does experience an inability to control the adduction move-ment of the arm.
REFERENCE Calis M, Akgun K, Birtane M, Karacan I,Calis H, Tuzun F.
Diagnostic values of clinical diagnostic tests in subacromial impingement syndrome.

units.title: TEST POSITIONING
units.summary: Position 1: The subject stands with arms relaxed at the sides. Position 2: The subject stands with hands on the hips and shoulders in 10 degrees of extension. Position 3: The subject stands with shoulders abducted to 90 degrees and maximally internally rotated.
summary_sentences: Position 1: The subject stands with arms relaxed at the sides.
Position 2: The subject stands with hands on the hips and shoulders in 10 degrees of extension.
Position 3: The subject stands with shoulders abducted to 90 degrees and maximally internally rotated.

units.title: ACTION
units.summary: Position 1: The examiner measures the distance from the inferior angle of the scapula (involved side) to the spinous process of the thoracic vertebra in the same horizontal plane (this vertebra will be used as the reference vertebra for all three positions) (Figure 3-6A). This is repeated on the uninvolved side. The difference between sides is used for the objective assessment.
summary_sentences: Position 1: The examiner measures the distance from the inferior angle of the scapula (involved side) to the spinous process of the thoracic vertebra in the same horizontal plane (this vertebra will be used as the reference vertebra for all three positions) (Figure 3-6A).
This is repeated on the uninvolved side.
The difference between sides is used for the objective assessment.

units.title: POSITIVE FINDING
units.summary: A side-to-side difference of >1.5 centimeters is considered a positive LSST, indicating scapular asymmetry secondary to weakness of the scapular stabilizers.
summary_sentences: A side-to-side difference of >1.5 centimeters is considered a positive LSST, indicating scapular asymmetry secondary to weakness of the scapular stabilizers.

units.title: SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS/COMMENTS
units.summary: The reliability, sensitivity, and specificity of this test in assessing/predicting shoulder dysfunction have been questioned. Because this test is considered a semi-dynamic test only, it may not accurately assess the stabilizing strength of the scapular muscles. It may more accurately assess general asymmetries, leading the clinician to fur-ther assess the underlying cause of these asymmetries (eg, motor con-trol, or lack there of; inflexibilities; thoracic spine/postural deviations;
summary_sentences: The reliability, sensitivity, and specificity of this test in assessing/predicting shoulder dysfunction have been questioned.
Because this test is considered a semi-dynamic test only, it may not accurately assess the stabilizing strength of the scapular muscles.

units.title: TEST POSITIONING
units.summary: The examiner stands next to the subject.
summary_sentences: The examiner stands next to the subject.

units.title: ACTION
units.summary: The subject is instructed to take one hand and touch the opposite shoulder. Repeat with the other hand to opposite side (Figure 3-7A). The subject is then instructed to place the arm overhead and reach behind the neck as if scratching the upper back.
summary_sentences: The subject is instructed to take one hand and touch the opposite shoulder.
Repeat with the other hand to opposite side (Figure 3-7A).
The subject is then instructed to place the arm overhead and reach behind the neck as if scratching the upper back.

units.title: POSITIVE FINDING
units.summary: Asymmetrical results from side to side are positive. The inability to touch the opposite shoulder is indicative of limited glenohumeral adduction, internal rotation, and horizontal flexion. Limits in scapular protraction may also produce asymmetrical results.
summary_sentences: Asymmetrical results from side to side are positive.
The inability to touch the opposite shoulder is indicative of limited glenohumeral adduction, internal rotation, and horizontal flexion.
Limits in scapular protraction may also produce asymmetrical results.

units.title: SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS/COMMENTS
units.summary: Each of these movements is an active test of the functional mobility of the shoulder. Care should be taken to isolate movements that are restricted. It is not uncommon for a subject to have slightly greater restriction on the dominant shoulder as compared to the nondominant shoulder due to increased muscle mass on the dominant side.
summary_sentences: Each of these movements is an active test of the functional mobility of the shoulder.
Care should be taken to isolate movements that are restricted.
It is not uncommon for a subject to have slightly greater restriction on the dominant shoulder as compared to the nondominant shoulder due to increased muscle mass on the dominant side.

units.title: TEST POSITIONING
units.summary: The examiner stands with one hand on the posteri-or aspect of the subject's shoulder to stabilize the trunk and the other hand grasping the subject's elbow on the test arm.
summary_sentences: The examiner stands with one hand on the posteri-or aspect of the subject's shoulder to stabilize the trunk and the other hand grasping the subject's elbow on the test arm.

units.title: ACTION
units.summary: With the subject's trunk stabilized, the examiner passively and max-imally horizontally adducts the test shoulder (Figure 3-8).
summary_sentences: With the subject's trunk stabilized, the examiner passively and max-imally horizontally adducts the test shoulder (Figure 3-8).

units.title: POSITIVE FINDING
units.summary: Superior shoulder pain is indicative of acromioclavicular joint pathology. Anterior shoulder pain is indicative of subscapularis, supraspinatus, and/or biceps long head pathology. Posterior shoulder pain is indicative of infraspinatus, teres minor, and/or posterior capsule pathology.
summary_sentences: Superior shoulder pain is indicative of acromioclavicular joint pathology.
Anterior shoulder pain is indicative of subscapularis, supraspinatus, and/or biceps long head pathology.
Posterior shoulder pain is indicative of infraspinatus, teres minor, and/or posterior capsule pathology.

units.title: TEST POSITIONING
units.summary: The subject lies supine on a table with the test shoulder placed in 90- 110 degrees of abduction and 10-15 degrees of extension. The test elbow is flexed to 90 degrees. The examiner stands with the distal hand grasping the subject's wrist and hand and the proximal hand grasping the subject's elbow (Figure 3-9A).
summary_sentences: The subject lies supine on a table with the test shoulder placed in 90- 110 degrees of abduction and 10-15 degrees of extension.
The test elbow is flexed to 90 degrees.
The examiner stands with the distal hand grasping the subject's wrist and hand and the proximal hand grasping the subject's elbow (Figure 3-9A).

units.title: ACTION
units.summary: The examiner slowly rotates the subject's shoulder into maximal external rotation (Figure 3-9B).
summary_sentences: The examiner slowly rotates the subject's shoulder into maximal external rotation (Figure 3-9B).

units.title: POSITIVE FINDING
units.summary: Reproduction of the subject's pain in the posterior aspect of the shoulder is indicative of rotator cuff and/or posterior labral pathology.
summary_sentences: Reproduction of the subject's pain in the posterior aspect of the shoulder is indicative of rotator cuff and/or posterior labral pathology.

units.title: SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS/COMMENTS
units.summary: This test should not be confused with the Apprehension Test or Relocation Test. The Posterior Impingement Test will reproduce poste-rior shoulder pain, while the Apprehension and Relocation Tests will reproduce anterior shoulder pain and apprehension. Clinically, the Posterior Impingement Test will often correlate highly with the subjec-tive complaints of posterior/superior shoulder pain during the late cock-ing to acceleration phase of throwing or swinging in the overhead ath-lete.
summary_sentences: This test should not be confused with the Apprehension Test or Relocation Test.
The Posterior Impingement Test will reproduce poste-rior shoulder pain, while the Apprehension and Relocation Tests will reproduce anterior shoulder pain and apprehension.

Clinically, the Posterior Impingement Test will often correlate highly with the subjec-tive complaints of posterior/superior shoulder pain during the late cock-ing to acceleration phase of throwing or swinging in the overhead ath-lete.

units.title: ACTION
units.summary: With the subject's scapula stabilized, the examiner passively and maximally forward flexes the test shoulder (Figure 3-10).
summary_sentences: With the subject's scapula stabilized, the examiner passively and maximally forward flexes the test shoulder (Figure 3-10).

units.title: POSITIVE FINDING
units.summary: Shoulder pain and apprehension are indicative of shoulder impinge-ment, particularly of the supraspinatus and biceps long head tendons.
summary_sentences: Shoulder pain and apprehension are indicative of shoulder impinge-ment, particularly of the supraspinatus and biceps long head tendons.

units.title: SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS/COMMENTS
units.summary: A false positive test may be elicited if the subject has limited forward flexion to the extent that anatomical impingement is not the limiting factor.
summary_sentences: A false positive test may be elicited if the subject has limited forward flexion to the extent that anatomical impingement is not the limiting factor.

units.title: TEST POSITIONING
units.summary: The subject sits or stands with both upper extremities relaxed. The examiner stands with one hand grasping the subject's elbow and the other hand grasping the subject's wrist, both on the test arm.
summary_sentences: The subject sits or stands with both upper extremities relaxed.
The examiner stands with one hand grasping the subject's elbow and the other hand grasping the subject's wrist, both on the test arm.

units.title: ACTION
units.summary: The examiner forward flexes the shoulder to 90 degrees and then internally rotates the subject's test shoulder (Figure 3-11).
summary_sentences: The examiner forward flexes the shoulder to 90 degrees and then internally rotates the subject's test shoulder (Figure 3-11).

units.title: POSITIVE FINDING
units.summary: Shoulder pain and apprehension are indicative of shoulder impinge-ment, particularly of the supraspinatus tendon.
summary_sentences: Shoulder pain and apprehension are indicative of shoulder impinge-ment, particularly of the supraspinatus tendon.

units.title: SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS/COMMENTS
units.summary: This test tends to be the most sensitive for assessing subacromial impingement.
summary_sentences: This test tends to be the most sensitive for assessing subacromial impingement.

units.title: TEST POSITIONING
units.summary: The subject sits with the involved arm relaxed at the side. The exam-iner stands in front of the subject, placing one hand on the proximal end of the subject's clavicle and the other hand on the spine of the scapula (Figure 3-12).
summary_sentences: The subject sits with the involved arm relaxed at the side.
The exam-iner stands in front of the subject, placing one hand on the proximal end of the subject's clavicle and the other hand on the spine of the scapula (Figure 3-12).

units.title: ACTION
units.summary: The examiner applies gentle inferior and posterior pressure on the clavicle, noting any movement at the sternoclavicular joint.
summary_sentences: The examiner applies gentle inferior and posterior pressure on the clavicle, noting any movement at the sternoclavicular joint.

units.title: POSITIVE FINDING
units.summary: Pain and/or movement of the clavicle indicates a sternoclavicular lig-ament sprain, possibly involving the costoclavicular ligament.
summary_sentences: Pain and/or movement of the clavicle indicates a sternoclavicular lig-ament sprain, possibly involving the costoclavicular ligament.

units.title: SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS/COMMENTS

units.title: TEST POSITIONING

summary_sentences: The subject lies supine on a table.

units.title: POSITIVE FINDING
units.summary: A positive finding for this test can be interpreted if the subject looks apprehensive or expresses feelings of apprehension toward further movement in the externally rotated direction. This test is used to mimic the positioning and movement of an anterior dislocation of the gleno-humeral joint, thus recreating a subject's episode of instability.

summary_sentences: Simple indication or reporting of apprehension to a movement does not necessarily indicate a dislocation of the glenohumeral joint.

summary_sentences: The examiner places the subject's involved shoulder in a position of 90 degrees of flexion and internal rotation while applying a posterior force through the long axis of the humerus (Figure 3-17).

units.title: POSITIVE FINDING
units.summary: Excessive inferior humeral head translation with a visible and/or palpable “step-off’ or “sulcus” deformity immediately inferior to the acromion (laterally) is indicative of inferior and/or multidirectional instability.
summary_sentences: Excessive inferior humeral head translation with a visible and/or palpable “step-off’ or “sulcus” deformity immediately inferior to the acromion (laterally) is indicative of inferior and/or multidirectional instability.

units.summary: A positive sulcus sign at rest may indicate excessive capsular stretch-ing. This may also be accompanied by a neurological stretch to struc-tures of the brachial plexus.

units.title: TEST POSITIONING
units.summary: The subject lies supine with the glenohumeral joint positioned at the edge of the table. The examiner stands next to the involved shoulder, placing one hand around the humerus below the surgical neck. The other hand stabilizes the scapula by placing the fingers behind the sub-ject on the spine of the scapula and the thumb over the coracoid process (Figure 3-19).

The other hand stabilizes the scapula by placing the fingers behind the sub-ject on the spine of the scapula and the thumb over the coracoid process (Figure 3-19).

units.title: ACTION
units.summary: The subject must remain relaxed while the examiner passively abducts the glenohumeral joint 70 to 80 degrees, forward flexes 0 to 10 degrees, and externally rotates 0 to 10 degrees. While stabilizing the scapula, the examiner firmly glides the head of the humerus anteriorly while applying slight distraction to the glenohumeral joint.
summary_sentences: The subject must remain relaxed while the examiner passively abducts the glenohumeral joint 70 to 80 degrees, forward flexes 0 to 10 degrees, and externally rotates 0 to 10 degrees.
While stabilizing the scapula, the examiner firmly glides the head of the humerus anteriorly while applying slight distraction to the glenohumeral joint.

units.title: POSITIVE FINDING
units.summary: Increased anterior translation of the humeral head relative to the scapula/glenoid fossa may be indicative of anterior instability. The sub-ject may exhibit apprehension if the test is positive. A bilateral compar-ison should be used for a more accurate assessment.

units.title: ACTION
units.summary: While stabilizing the scapula, the examiner applies downward pres-sure, pushing the humeral head posteriorly. The examiner notes any posterior movement of the humeral head (Figure 3-20B).

The examiner notes any posterior movement of the humeral head (Figure 3-20B).

units.title: POSITIVE FINDING
units.summary: Increased posterior instability of the humeral head relative to the scapula/glenoid fossa may be indicative of posterior instability. The sub-ject may exhibit apprehension if the test is positive.

units.title: TEST POSITIONING
units.summary: The subject lies supine with the test shoulder in 90 degrees of abduc-tion and full external rotation. The examiner stands with the distal hand grasping the subject's wrist and hand. The examiner's proximal hand is placed over the subject's humeral head (anteriorly) (Figure 3-21).
summary_sentences: The subject lies supine with the test shoulder in 90 degrees of abduc-tion and full external rotation.
The examiner stands with the distal hand grasping the subject's wrist and hand.
The examiner's proximal hand is placed over the subject's humeral head (anteriorly) (Figure 3-21).

units.title: ACTION
units.summary: The examiner applies a posterior force to the humeral head, while the examiner externally rotates the subject's humerus
summary_sentences: The examiner applies a posterior force to the humeral head, while the examiner externally rotates the subject's humerus

units.title: POSITIVE FINDING
units.summary: A reduction of pain and apprehension, and commonly an increase in shoulder external rotation, are indicative of anterior instability.
summary_sentences: A reduction of pain and apprehension, and commonly an increase in shoulder external rotation, are indicative of anterior instability.

units.title: SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS/COMMENTS
units.summary: This test should be performed immediately following the apprehen-sion test. Pain associated with the Jobe relocation test that follows a positive anterior apprehension test may be associated with any number of pathologies not limited to anterior instability. However, if pain is seen with an anterior apprehension test and subsides with a subsequent Jobe relocation test, it is quite possible that any pain was in fact associ-ated with a greater than normal anterior gliding of the humeral head.

units.title: TEST POSITIONING
units.summary: The subject lies supine with the test shoulder in 90 degrees of abduc-tion and full external rotation. The examiner stands with the distal hand grasping the subject's wrist and hand and the proximal hand placed over the subject's humeral head (anteriorly), applying a posteriorly-direct force to the humeral head (Figure 3-22A).

The examiner stands with the distal hand grasping the subject's wrist and hand and the proximal hand placed over the subject's humeral head (anteriorly), applying a posteriorly-direct force to the humeral head (Figure 3-22A).

units.title: ACTION
units.summary: The examiner quickly removes the proximal hand from the humeral head (Figure 3-22B).
summary_sentences: The examiner quickly removes the proximal hand from the humeral head (Figure 3-22B).

units.title: POSITIVE FINDING
units.summary: A sudden return of symptoms that were elicited from the Apprehen-sion Test is indicative of anterior instability.
summary_sentences: A sudden return of symptoms that were elicited from the Apprehen-sion Test is indicative of anterior instability.

units.title: SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS/COMMENTS
units.summary: The Surprise Test is merely an extension of the Relocation Test, and should therefore be performed immediately following the Apprehen-sion and Relocation Tests, respectively. If the subject demonstrates severe apprehension and instability symptoms with the Apprehension Test, the Surprise Test should not be performed so as not to traumatize (or lose rapport with) the subject.

units.title: TEST POSITIONING
units.summary: The subject stands with the involved arm abducted to 90 degrees. The elbow is extended and allowed to rest on the examiner's shoulder. The examiner stands to the side of the subject and clasps his hands together around the upper and middle thirds of the humerus.
summary_sentences: The subject stands with the involved arm abducted to 90 degrees.
The elbow is extended and allowed to rest on the examiner's shoulder.
The examiner stands to the side of the subject and clasps his hands together around the upper and middle thirds of the humerus.

units.title: ACTION
units.summary: The examiner attempts to glide the humerus in an anterior and infe-rior direction (Figure 3-23).
summary_sentences: The examiner attempts to glide the humerus in an anterior and infe-rior direction (Figure 3-23).

units.title: POSITIVE FINDING
units.summary: Excessive gliding of the humerus (as compared to the noninvolved side) may be indicative of anterior and/or inferior glenohumeral insta-bility.
summary_sentences: Excessive gliding of the humerus (as compared to the noninvolved side) may be indicative of anterior and/or inferior glenohumeral insta-bility.

units.title: SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS/COMMENTS
units.summary: The subject may appear to be apprehensive when performing this test. If so, the examiner can only conclude that the test is not sensitive enough to assess instability unless the examiner is able to judge acces-sory motion compared to the uninvolved side. Apprehension alone can-not be used to predict glenohumeral instability.

The examiner stands slightly behind the subject while stabilizing the clavicle and scapula with one hand. With the other hand, the examiner grasps the subject's humeral head with the thumb posterior-ly.

units.title: ACTION
units.summary: The examiner places an axial load along the shaft of the humerus (load) in an attempt to compress the humeral head into the glenoid fossa. With the load applied, the examiner translates the humeral head, first anteriorly (shift) and then posteriorly (shift).
summary_sentences: The examiner places an axial load along the shaft of the humerus (load) in an attempt to compress the humeral head into the glenoid fossa.
With the load applied, the examiner translates the humeral head, first anteriorly (shift) and then posteriorly (shift).

units.title: POSITIVE FINDING
units.summary: An anterior or posterior translation of the humeral head greater than 25% of the diameter of the humeral head when a load is applied is con-sidered to be a positive test. The test should be repeated bilaterally for comparative findings.
summary_sentences: An anterior or posterior translation of the humeral head greater than 25% of the diameter of the humeral head when a load is applied is con-sidered to be a positive test.
The test should be repeated bilaterally for comparative findings.

units.title: SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS/COMMENTS
units.summary: Translation between 25% and 50% has been described as being a grade |positive test. Greater than 50% translation associated with a sub-sequent reduction of the humeral head is considered grade II, while the same amount of translation without reduction is recognized as grade III] and the most serious type of a shift.

Greater than 50% translation associated with a sub-sequent reduction of the humeral head is considered grade II, while the same amount of translation without reduction is recognized as grade III] and the most serious type of a shift.

units.title: TEST POSITIONING

units.title: ACTION

summary_sentences: The examiner applies compression to the glenoid labrum while attempting to rotate the humeral head 360 degrees around the surface of the glenoid fossa.

units.title: POSITIVE FINDING
units.summary: A positive finding of a grinding or clunking sensation may be indica-tive of a glenoid labrum tear to the specific location, which is being compressed.
summary_sentences: A positive finding of a grinding or clunking sensation may be indica-tive of a glenoid labrum tear to the specific location, which is being compressed.

units.summary: This test should be done carefully, since the application of excessive pressure combined with rotation may further damage the glenoid labrum.
summary_sentences: This test should be done carefully, since the application of excessive pressure combined with rotation may further damage the glenoid labrum.

This test is most appropriate for assessing superior labral tears since the inferior portion of the labrum is not in contact with the humeral head while the humerus is positioned in full abduction and external rotation. Due to the nature of this anatomi-cal positioning, it is quite possible to experience a false negative test if the subject has an inferior labral tear.

units.summary: With the subject standing, the examiner places the distal hand on the subject's elbow and the proximal hand on the subject's proximal humerus and then passively elevates the subject's shoulder to 160 degrees in the scapular plane.
summary_sentences: With the subject standing, the examiner places the distal hand on the subject's elbow and the proximal hand on the subject's proximal humerus and then passively elevates the subject's shoulder to 160 degrees in the scapular plane.

units.summary: The subject sits or stands with the test shoulder in 90 degrees of for-ward flexion, 30 to 45 degrees of horizontal adduction, and maximal internal rotation. The examiner stands with one hand grasping the sub-ject's test wrist (medially) (Figure 3-28A).

summary_sentences: The subject horizontally adducts and flexes the test shoulder against the examiner's manual resistance (Figure 3-28B).

units.summary: The O'Brien test is considered to be the most accurate test for assess-ing SLAP lesions; however, the sensitivity of this and other SLAP lesion tests are questionable. To more closely simulate the eccentric traction associated with the mechanism of injury related to SLAP lesions, the examiner may wish to slowly move the subject's arm from a flexed to an extended position while resisting horizontal adduction and shoulder flexion.

units.title: SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS/COMMENTS
units.summary: If pain is in the neck on the side toward lateral flexion, a pinched nerve or facet joint impingement may exist. This test should not be per-formed if a cervical fracture or dislocation is suspected.

units.summary: The subject must be completely relaxed, as contraction of the hip flexor muscles could increase the stress placed on the lumbar spine and sacroiliac joint, thus creating false positive findings. Additionally, dur-ing the unilateral straight leg raise test, pain may be noted in the con-tralateral leg and/or lumbar spine. This finding should be referred to as a positive crossed straight leg raise test.

Additionally, dur-ing the unilateral straight leg raise test, pain may be noted in the con-tralateral leg and/or lumbar spine.
This finding should be referred to as a positive crossed straight leg raise test.
