units.title: TEST POSITIONING
units.summary: The subject lies supine with both hips and knees extended. The examiner is standing with the distal hand or forearm around or under the subject's heels and the proximal hand on the subject's distal thighs (anteriorly) to maintain knee extension.
summary_sentences: The subject lies supine with both hips and knees extended.
The examiner is standing with the distal hand or forearm around or under the subject's heels and the proximal hand on the subject's distal thighs (anteriorly) to maintain knee extension.

units.title: ACTION
units.summary: With the subject completely relaxed, slowly raise the legs until pain or tightness is noted (Figure 7-8).
summary_sentences: With the subject completely relaxed, slowly raise the legs until pain or tightness is noted (Figure 7-8).

units.title: POSITIVE FINDING
units.summary: Low back pain occurring at hip flexion angles less than 70 degrees is indicative of sacroiliac joint involvement. Low back pain occurring at hip flexion angles greater than 70 degrees is indicative of lumbar spine involvement.
summary_sentences: Low back pain occurring at hip flexion angles less than 70 degrees is indicative of sacroiliac joint involvement.
Low back pain occurring at hip flexion angles greater than 70 degrees is indicative of lumbar spine involvement.

units.title: SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS/COMMENTS
units.summary: The examiner must utilize proper body mechanics when performing this test in order to avoid injury secondary to lifting the weight of both legs. The examiner should also note any excessive pelvic motion that may indicate the subject's discomfort and/or mechanical compensation associated with the test.
summary_sentences: The examiner must utilize proper body mechanics when performing this test in order to avoid injury secondary to lifting the weight of both legs.
The examiner should also note any excessive pelvic motion that may indicate the subject's discomfort and/or mechanical compensation associated with the test.

units.title: TEST POSITIONING
units.summary: The subject lies supine on a table. The examiner places one hand on the anterior aspect of the uninvolved leg slightly superior to the knee and the other hand around the heel of the ipsilateral calcaneus.
summary_sentences: The subject lies supine on a table.
The examiner places one hand on the anterior aspect of the uninvolved leg slightly superior to the knee and the other hand around the heel of the ipsilateral calcaneus.

units.title: ACTION
units.summary: The examiner passively flexes the subject's uninvolved hip while maintaining the knee in an extended position (Figure 7-9).
summary_sentences: The examiner passively flexes the subject's uninvolved hip while maintaining the knee in an extended position (Figure 7-9).

units.title: POSITIVE FINDING
units.summary: Complaints of pain on the involved side indicate a positive test and may be related to vertebral disk damage.
summary_sentences: Complaints of pain on the involved side indicate a positive test and may be related to vertebral disk damage.

units.title: SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS/COMMENTS
units.summary: This test was first described by Fajerstajn but is also known as a pros-trate leg raising test, Lhermitt's test, or a cross-over sign. When this test is performed, a dural stretch is applied to both sides of the lower extremity. Therefore, complaints of pain may be noted in a radicular manner.
summary_sentences: This test was first described by Fajerstajn but is also known as a pros-trate leg raising test, Lhermitt's test, or a cross-over sign.
When this test is performed, a dural stretch is applied to both sides of the lower extremity.
Therefore, complaints of pain may be noted in a radicular manner.

units.title: TEST POSITIONING
units.summary: The subject sits on the end of the table and leans forward while the examiner holds the head and chin upright (Figure 7-10A).
summary_sentences: The subject sits on the end of the table and leans forward while the examiner holds the head and chin upright (Figure 7-10A).

units.title: ACTION
units.summary: Any symptomatic changes reported by the subject are noted. The examiner then flexes the subject's neck and assesses for any changes in symptoms (Figure 7-10B). If no changes are noted, the examiner pas-sively extends one of the subject's knees (Figure 7-10C).
summary_sentences: Any symptomatic changes reported by the subject are noted.
The examiner then flexes the subject's neck and assesses for any changes in symptoms (Figure 7-10B).
If no changes are noted, the examiner pas-sively extends one of the subject's knees (Figure 7-10C).

units.title: POSITIVE FINDING
units.summary: A complaint of sciatic-type pain or any reproduction of symptoms is indicative of a positive test.
summary_sentences: A complaint of sciatic-type pain or any reproduction of symptoms is indicative of a positive test.

units.title: SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS/COMMENTS
units.summary: The examiner should note the location of the symptomatic changes, as this is often the site of a dural stretch. Others have described this test whereby the subject actively moves the knee and ankle, as opposed to passive movement.
summary_sentences: The examiner should note the location of the symptomatic changes, as this is often the site of a dural stretch.
Others have described this test whereby the subject actively moves the knee and ankle, as opposed to passive movement.

units.title: TEST POSITIONING
units.summary: The subject lies supine with both knees fully flexed against the chest and the buttocks near the table edge. The examiner stands with one hand on the subject's lumbar spine or iliac crest to monitor lumbar lordosis or pelvic tilt, respectively (Figure 7-11A).
summary_sentences: The subject lies supine with both knees fully flexed against the chest and the buttocks near the table edge.
The examiner stands with one hand on the subject's lumbar spine or iliac crest to monitor lumbar lordosis or pelvic tilt, respectively (Figure 7-11A).

units.title: ACTION
units.summary: The subject slowly lowers the test leg until the leg is fully relaxed or until either anterior pelvic tilting or an increase in lumbar lordosis occurs (Figure 7-11B).
summary_sentences: The subject slowly lowers the test leg until the leg is fully relaxed or until either anterior pelvic tilting or an increase in lumbar lordosis occurs (Figure 7-11B).

units.title: POSITIVE FINDING
units.summary: A lack of hip extension with knee flexion greater than 45 degrees is indicative of iliopsoas muscle tightness. Full hip extension with knee flex-ion less than 45 degrees is indicative of rectus femoris muscle tightness. A lack of hip extension with knee flexion less than 45 degrees is indicative of iliopsoas and rectus femoris muscle tightness.
summary_sentences: A lack of hip extension with knee flexion greater than 45 degrees is indicative of iliopsoas muscle tightness.
Full hip extension with knee flex-ion less than 45 degrees is indicative of rectus femoris muscle tightness.
A lack of hip extension with knee flexion less than 45 degrees is indicative of iliopsoas and rectus femoris muscle tightness.

units.title: SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS/COMMENTS
units.summary: Increases in anterior pelvic tilt and lumbar lordosis must be eliminated in order to prevent false negative findings. To further confirm this assess-ment, the examiner can simply apply pressure on the lower leg in an effort to lower it back to the table. A return of lumbar lordosis will indi-cate a positive finding.
summary_sentences: Increases in anterior pelvic tilt and lumbar lordosis must be eliminated in order to prevent false negative findings.
To further confirm this assess-ment, the examiner can simply apply pressure on the lower leg in an effort to lower it back to the table.
A return of lumbar lordosis will indi-cate a positive finding.

units.title: TEST POSITIONING
units.summary: The subject lies prone and the examiner stands with the thumb (Figure 7-12A) or hypothenar eminence (specifically the pisiform) over the spinous process of a lumbar vertebra (Figure 7-12B).
summary_sentences: The subject lies prone and the examiner stands with the thumb (Figure 7-12A) or hypothenar eminence (specifically the pisiform) over the spinous process of a lumbar vertebra (Figure 7-12B).

units.title: ACTION
units.summary: Apply a downward “springing” force through the spinous process of each vertebra to assess posterior-anterior motion. This action should be repeated for each transverse process to assess rotary motion.
summary_sentences: Apply a downward “springing” force through the spinous process of each vertebra to assess posterior-anterior motion.
This action should be repeated for each transverse process to assess rotary motion.

units.title: POSITIVE FINDING
units.summary: Increases or decreases in motion at one vertebra compared to anoth-er are indicative of hypermobility or hypomobility, respectively.
summary_sentences: Increases or decreases in motion at one vertebra compared to anoth-er are indicative of hypermobility or hypomobility, respectively.

units.title: SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS/COMMENTS
units.summary: Rotational accessory movement can be compared at each level by performing this test to the transverse process on each side of one verte-bral level.
summary_sentences: Rotational accessory movement can be compared at each level by performing this test to the transverse process on each side of one verte-bral level.

units.title: TEST POSITIONING
units.summary: The subject stands on one lower extremity (Figures 7-13A and 7-13B).
summary_sentences: The subject stands on one lower extremity (Figures 7-13A and 7-13B).

units.title: ACTION
units.summary: The subject remains in this position for approximately 10 seconds and then switches extremities.
summary_sentences: The subject remains in this position for approximately 10 seconds and then switches extremities.

units.title: POSITIVE FINDING
units.summary: A positive finding is seen when the pelvis on the unsupported side drops noticeably lower than the pelvis on the supported side. This indi-cates a weakness of the gluteus medius muscle on the supported side.
summary_sentences: A positive finding is seen when the pelvis on the unsupported side drops noticeably lower than the pelvis on the supported side.
This indi-cates a weakness of the gluteus medius muscle on the supported side.

units.title: SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS/COMMENTS
units.summary: With a negative test, the gluteus medius on the supported side will perform a reverse action since the supported femur is stabilized. This will allow for the unsupported pelvis to remain level with the supported pelvis. With a weak gluteus medius on the supported side, the unsup-ported pelvis drops as the muscles fatigues.
summary_sentences: With a negative test, the gluteus medius on the supported side will perform a reverse action since the supported femur is stabilized.
This will allow for the unsupported pelvis to remain level with the supported pelvis.
With a weak gluteus medius on the supported side, the unsup-ported pelvis drops as the muscles fatigues.

units.title: TEST POSITIONING
units.summary: The subject stands on one leg with the sole of the nonweightbearing foot resting on the medial aspect of the knee of the weightbearing limb (Figure 7-14A).
summary_sentences: The subject stands on one leg with the sole of the nonweightbearing foot resting on the medial aspect of the knee of the weightbearing limb (Figure 7-14A).

units.title: ACTION
units.summary: The subject maintains balance on one leg and then simultaneously performs a slight lumbar extension movement (Figure 7-14B). The test is repeated bilaterally.
summary_sentences: The subject maintains balance on one leg and then simultaneously performs a slight lumbar extension movement (Figure 7-14B).
The test is repeated bilaterally.

units.title: POSITIVE FINDING
units.summary: Complaints of pain in the lumbar region may be related to the pars interarticularis region, which is sometimes associated with spondyloly-
summary_sentences: Complaints of pain in the lumbar region may be related to the pars interarticularis region, which is sometimes associated with spondyloly-

units.title: SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS/COMMENTS
units.summary: This test is also referred to as the one-leg standing lumbar extension test. The examiner should assess the level of each pelvis during the test. Changes in the pelvic levels related to gluteus medius muscle weakness may present to the examiner as a false indicator of poor proprioception.
summary_sentences: This test is also referred to as the one-leg standing lumbar extension test.
The examiner should assess the level of each pelvis during the test.
Changes in the pelvic levels related to gluteus medius muscle weakness may present to the examiner as a false indicator of poor proprioception.

units.title: TEST POSITIONING
units.summary: The subject stands with the sacroiliac joint exposed. The examiner stands behind the subject with the thumbs over the posterior superior iliac spines (Figure 8-1A). The examiner may then leave the one thumb over the sacral spinous process and move the other thumb to the ischial tuberosity.
summary_sentences: The subject stands with the sacroiliac joint exposed.
The examiner stands behind the subject with the thumbs over the posterior superior iliac spines (Figure 8-1A).
The examiner may then leave the one thumb over the sacral spinous process and move the other thumb to the ischial tuberosity.

units.title: ACTION
units.summary: The examiner should note whether the posterior superior iliac spines are level. Positive FInpinG 1 If the posterior iliac spines are not level, the sacroiliac joints are asymmetrical, indicating fixation on one side or the other. The subject is then instructed to actively flex each hip one at a time with the knee bent to 90 degrees.
summary_sentences: The examiner should note whether the posterior superior iliac spines are level.
Positive FInpinG 1 If the posterior iliac spines are not level, the sacroiliac joints are asymmetrical, indicating fixation on one side or the other.
The subject is then instructed to actively flex each hip one at a time with the knee bent to 90 degrees.

units.title: POSITIVE FINDING
units.summary: When the subject flexes each hip, the thumb over the posterior supe-rior iliac spine should drop relative to the spinous process. If there is no change or the thumb moves superiorly, hypomobility is indicated. When the subject again flexes each hip, the thumb over the ischial tuberosity should move inferiorly.
summary_sentences: When the subject flexes each hip, the thumb over the posterior supe-rior iliac spine should drop relative to the spinous process.
If there is no change or the thumb moves superiorly, hypomobility is indicated.
When the subject again flexes each hip, the thumb over the ischial tuberosity should move inferiorly.

units.title: SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS/COMMENTS
units.summary: Having the subject actively flex one hip and then comparing the level of the PSIS on each side has been described as a Gillet test. Decreased or minimal inferior movement of the sacroiliac joint on the flexed side indicates a hypomobile joint. TeEsT POSITIONING 2 The examiner then places one thumb over the posterior superior iliac spine on the right or left side, and the other thumb over the S2 spinous process.
summary_sentences: Having the subject actively flex one hip and then comparing the level of the PSIS on each side has been described as a Gillet test.
Decreased or minimal inferior movement of the sacroiliac joint on the flexed side indicates a hypomobile joint.
TeEsT POSITIONING 2 The examiner then places one thumb over the posterior superior iliac spine on the right or left side, and the other thumb over the S2 spinous process.

units.title: TEST POSITIONING
units.summary: The subject stands while the examiner palpates the posterior superi-or iliac spine bilaterally.
summary_sentences: The subject stands while the examiner palpates the posterior superi-or iliac spine bilaterally.

units.title: ACTION
units.summary: The subject flexes one hip and brings the knee to the chest while the examiner maintains palpation to each PSIS and assesses overall sacroili-ac movement (Figure 8-2A).
summary_sentences: The subject flexes one hip and brings the knee to the chest while the examiner maintains palpation to each PSIS and assesses overall sacroili-ac movement (Figure 8-2A).

units.title: POSITIVE FINDING
units.summary: A positive sign is noted if the PSIS on the ipsilateral side of the knee being flexed does not move or moves minimally in the inferior direction (Figure 8-2B).
summary_sentences: A positive sign is noted if the PSIS on the ipsilateral side of the knee being flexed does not move or moves minimally in the inferior direction (Figure 8-2B).

units.title: SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS/COMMENTS
units.summary: The PSIS on the side of the hip being flexed should move slightly anteriorly during active hip flexion.
summary_sentences: The PSIS on the side of the hip being flexed should move slightly anteriorly during active hip flexion.

units.title: TEST POSITIONING
units.summary: The examiner stands next to the subject and, with the arms crossed, places the heel of both hands on the subject's anterior superior iliac spines (Figure 8-3A). The examiner stands next to the subject and places both hands, one on top of the other, directly over the subject's iliac crest. Repeat on the other side (Figure 8-3B).
summary_sentences: The examiner stands next to the subject and, with the arms crossed, places the heel of both hands on the subject's anterior superior iliac spines (Figure 8-3A).
The examiner stands next to the subject and places both hands, one on top of the other, directly over the subject's iliac crest.
Repeat on the other side (Figure 8-3B).

units.title: ACTION
units.summary: The examiner applies outward and downward pressure with the heel of the hands. The examiner applies downward pressure. The examiner applies inward and downward pressure.
summary_sentences: The examiner applies outward and downward pressure with the heel of the hands.
The examiner applies downward pressure.
The examiner applies inward and downward pressure.

units.title: POSITIVE FINDING
units.summary: Unilateral pain at the sacroiliac joint or in the gluteal or leg region indicates an anterior sacroiliac ligament sprain. Increased pain or pressure is indicative of sacroiliac joint pathology, possibly involving the posterior sacroiliac ligaments. Pain at the sacroiliac joint is indicative of sacroiliac joint pathology.
summary_sentences: Unilateral pain at the sacroiliac joint or in the gluteal or leg region indicates an anterior sacroiliac ligament sprain.
Increased pain or pressure is indicative of sacroiliac joint pathology, possibly involving the posterior sacroiliac ligaments.
Pain at the sacroiliac joint is indicative of sacroiliac joint pathology.

units.title: SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS/COMMENTS
units.summary: The subject may complain of pain that could be related to sacroiliac joint compression. The subject may complain of pain that could be related to sacroiliac joint distraction or gapping. REFERENCE Levin U, Nilsson-Wikmar L, Stenstrom CH, Lundeberg T.
summary_sentences: The subject may complain of pain that could be related to sacroiliac joint compression.
The subject may complain of pain that could be related to sacroiliac joint distraction or gapping.
REFERENCE Levin U, Nilsson-Wikmar L, Stenstrom CH, Lundeberg T.

units.title: ACTION
units.summary: The examiner compresses downward and inward at a 45-degree angle along the iliac crest and anterior superior iliac spine bilaterally.
summary_sentences: The examiner compresses downward and inward at a 45-degree angle along the iliac crest and anterior superior iliac spine bilaterally.

units.title: POSITIVE FINDING
units.summary: Subjective complaints of pain are noted as positive findings and may be found anteriorly or posteriorly.
summary_sentences: Subjective complaints of pain are noted as positive findings and may be found anteriorly or posteriorly.

units.title: SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS/COMMENTS
units.summary: This test assesses the stability of the posterior sacroiliac ligaments but also directly applies compressive forces to the anterior sacroiliac joint. Thus, the location of pain should be noted and correlated with any additional findings.
summary_sentences: This test assesses the stability of the posterior sacroiliac ligaments but also directly applies compressive forces to the anterior sacroiliac joint.
Thus, the location of pain should be noted and correlated with any additional findings.

units.title: TEST POSITIONING
units.summary: The subject lies prone on the table.
summary_sentences: The subject lies prone on the table.

units.title: ACTION
units.summary: The examiner passively flexes the subject's knee to 90 degrees while simultaneously extending the ipsilateral hip (Figure 8-5A).
summary_sentences: The examiner passively flexes the subject's knee to 90 degrees while simultaneously extending the ipsilateral hip (Figure 8-5A).

units.title: POSITIVE FINDING
units.summary: A reporting of pain during this test is considered to be a positive sign. Pain in the sacroiliac joint may be related to anterior sacroiliac ligament pathology. Pain in the anterior thigh region may be related to hip flex-or musculature tightness or femoral nerve tension.
summary_sentences: A reporting of pain during this test is considered to be a positive sign.
Pain in the sacroiliac joint may be related to anterior sacroiliac ligament pathology.
Pain in the anterior thigh region may be related to hip flex-or musculature tightness or femoral nerve tension.

units.title: SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS/COMMENTS
units.summary: The examiner should pay attention to the position of the subject's trunk, as trunk rotation may be used to compensate for positions of dis-comfort. Compensatory movement such as trunk rotation may result in a false negative test finding (Figure 8-5B).
summary_sentences: The examiner should pay attention to the position of the subject's trunk, as trunk rotation may be used to compensate for positions of dis-comfort.
Compensatory movement such as trunk rotation may result in a false negative test finding (Figure 8-5B).

units.title: TEST POSITIONING
units.summary: The subject lies on the side of the uninvolved leg (lower leg). With the involved leg (upper leg) in slight hyperextension, the subject then flexes the knee of the uninvolved side toward the chest.
summary_sentences: The subject lies on the side of the uninvolved leg (lower leg).
With the involved leg (upper leg) in slight hyperextension, the subject then flexes the knee of the uninvolved side toward the chest.

units.title: ACTION
units.summary: The examiner stabilizes the subject's pelvis and further extends the subject's involved leg (Figure 8-6).
summary_sentences: The examiner stabilizes the subject's pelvis and further extends the subject's involved leg (Figure 8-6).

units.title: POSITIVE FINDING
units.summary: Pain in the sacroiliac region is considered a positive finding and may be associated with sacroiliac joint dysfunction.
summary_sentences: Pain in the sacroiliac region is considered a positive finding and may be associated with sacroiliac joint dysfunction.

units.title: SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS/COMMENTS
units.summary: The subject may report pain in the hip or anterior thigh region. This may be related to hip joint pathology, anterior thigh musculature ten-sion, or L4 nerve root tension. This test can be performed with the sub-ject in a supine position, however, the examiner should be cautious of a false negative test due to the inability of obtaining enough involved leg hip extension.
summary_sentences: The subject may report pain in the hip or anterior thigh region.
This may be related to hip joint pathology, anterior thigh musculature ten-sion, or L4 nerve root tension.

This test can be performed with the sub-ject in a supine position, however, the examiner should be cautious of a false negative test due to the inability of obtaining enough involved leg hip extension.

units.title: TEST POSITIONING
units.summary: The subject lies supine on the table.
summary_sentences: The subject lies supine on the table.

units.title: ACTION
units.summary: The examiner passively flexes, abducts, and externally rotates the involved leg until the foot rests on the top of the knee of the nonin-volved lower extremity (Figure 8-7A). The examiner then slowly abducts the involved lower extremity, bringing the knee closer toward the table (Figure 8-7B).
summary_sentences: The examiner passively flexes, abducts, and externally rotates the involved leg until the foot rests on the top of the knee of the nonin-volved lower extremity (Figure 8-7A).
The examiner then slowly abducts the involved lower extremity, bringing the knee closer toward the table (Figure 8-7B).

units.title: POSITIVE FINDING
units.summary: A positive finding is revealed when the involved lower extremity does not abduct below the level of the noninvolved lower extremity. This may be indicative of iliopsoas, sacroiliac, or even hip joint abnor-malities.
summary_sentences: A positive finding is revealed when the involved lower extremity does not abduct below the level of the noninvolved lower extremity.
This may be indicative of iliopsoas, sacroiliac, or even hip joint abnor-malities.

units.title: SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS/COMMENTS
units.summary: FABER is an acronym for the initial positioning of the subject (flex-ion = F, abduction = AB, external rotation = ER).
summary_sentences: FABER is an acronym for the initial positioning of the subject (flex-ion = F, abduction = AB, external rotation = ER).

units.title: TEST POSITIONING
units.summary: The subject lies supine with both hips and knees extended, and the examiner stands with the thumbs on the subject's medial malleoli (Figure 8-8A).
summary_sentences: The subject lies supine with both hips and knees extended, and the examiner stands with the thumbs on the subject's medial malleoli (Figure 8-8A).

units.title: ACTION
units.summary: The examiner passively flexes both knees and hips (Figure 8-8B) and then fully extends and compares the position of the medial malleoli rel-ative to each other (Figure 8-8C). The subject then slowly assumes the long-sitting position, and malleolar position is re-assessed (Figure 8-8D).
summary_sentences: The examiner passively flexes both knees and hips (Figure 8-8B) and then fully extends and compares the position of the medial malleoli rel-ative to each other (Figure 8-8C).
The subject then slowly assumes the long-sitting position, and malleolar position is re-assessed (Figure 8-8D).

units.title: POSITIVE FINDING
units.summary: A leg that appears longer in supine position but shorter in long-sit-ting is indicative of an ipsilateral anteriorly rotated ilium. Conversely, a leg that appears shorter in supine position but longer in long-sitting is indicative of an ipsilateral posteriorly rotated ilium.
summary_sentences: A leg that appears longer in supine position but shorter in long-sit-ting is indicative of an ipsilateral anteriorly rotated ilium.
Conversely, a leg that appears shorter in supine position but longer in long-sitting is indicative of an ipsilateral posteriorly rotated ilium.

units.title: SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS/COMMENTS
units.summary: Marking the reference point of measurement on the malleolli with a pen may increase the reliability when comparing positions of leg length. Validation of the long-sitting test on subjects with iliosacral dysfunction.
summary_sentences: Marking the reference point of measurement on the malleolli with a pen may increase the reliability when comparing positions of leg length.
Validation of the long-sitting test on subjects with iliosacral dysfunction.

units.title: TEST POSITIONING
units.summary: The examiner stands on the involved side and passively flexes and adducts the subject's hip. The subject's knee is also placed in full flexion (Figure 9-1A).
summary_sentences: The examiner stands on the involved side and passively flexes and adducts the subject's hip.
The subject's knee is also placed in full flexion (Figure 9-1A).

units.title: ACTION
units.summary: The examiner applies downward pressure along the shaft of the femur while simultaneously adducting and externally rotating the hip (Figure 9-1B). The examiner then adducts and internally rotates the hip while maintaining downward pressure (Figure 9-1C). This movement is repeated two to three times while the examiner notes any unusual move-ment (ie, catching, grinding) or subject apprehension.
summary_sentences: The examiner applies downward pressure along the shaft of the femur while simultaneously adducting and externally rotating the hip (Figure 9-1B).
The examiner then adducts and internally rotates the hip while maintaining downward pressure (Figure 9-1C).
This movement is repeated two to three times while the examiner notes any unusual move-ment (ie, catching, grinding) or subject apprehension.

units.title: POSITIVE FINDING
units.summary: Pain or apprehension is indicative of hip joint pathology, such as arthritis, osteochondral defects, avascular necrosis, or acetabular labrum defects.
summary_sentences: Pain or apprehension is indicative of hip joint pathology, such as arthritis, osteochondral defects, avascular necrosis, or acetabular labrum defects.

units.title: SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS/COMMENTS
units.summary: This test is not very specific for identifying structural damage and should be used with caution to avoid causing further pain and/or tissue damage. Imaging tests are helpful tools to use in follow-up of a positive hip scour test accompanied by unexplained hip joint and/or radiating leg pain.
summary_sentences: This test is not very specific for identifying structural damage and should be used with caution to avoid causing further pain and/or tissue damage.
Imaging tests are helpful tools to use in follow-up of a positive hip scour test accompanied by unexplained hip joint and/or radiating leg pain.

units.title: TEST POSITIONING
units.summary: The subject is lying prone with the affected leg’s knee flexed to 90 degrees. The examiner stands on the involved side and palpates the greater trochanter (Figure 9-2A).
summary_sentences: The subject is lying prone with the affected leg’s knee flexed to 90 degrees.
The examiner stands on the involved side and palpates the greater trochanter (Figure 9-2A).

units.title: ACTION
units.summary: The examiner then passively internally and externally rotates the femur until the greater trochanter is parallel with the examining table (Figure 9-2B). At this point, the subject is asked to hold the hip in this position while the examiner measures the angle between the long axis of the lower leg and the perpendicular axis to the table with a goniome-ter (Figure 9-2C).
summary_sentences: The examiner then passively internally and externally rotates the femur until the greater trochanter is parallel with the examining table (Figure 9-2B).

At this point, the subject is asked to hold the hip in this position while the examiner measures the angle between the long axis of the lower leg and the perpendicular axis to the table with a goniome-ter (Figure 9-2C).

units.title: POSITIVE FINDING
units.summary: If the measured angle is greater than 15 degrees, femoral anteversion is indicated. If the measured angle is less than 8 degrees, femoral retro-version is indicated. Increased femoral anteversion leads to toeing-in and squinting patellae.
summary_sentences: If the measured angle is greater than 15 degrees, femoral anteversion is indicated.
If the measured angle is less than 8 degrees, femoral retro-version is indicated.
Increased femoral anteversion leads to toeing-in and squinting patellae.

units.title: SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS/COMMENTS
units.summary: A second examiner may be useful to hold the subject's hip and leg in the designated position while the first examiner measures the angle. This test is also known as the Ryder method for measuring femoral anteversion and retroversion.
summary_sentences: A second examiner may be useful to hold the subject's hip and leg in the designated position while the first examiner measures the angle.
This test is also known as the Ryder method for measuring femoral anteversion and retroversion.

units.title: TEST POSITIONING
units.summary: Test subject lies supine, stabilizing both hips at 90 degrees of flexion with both hands. The knees are bent in a relaxed position. The examin-er stands next to the subject (Figure 9-3A).
summary_sentences: Test subject lies supine, stabilizing both hips at 90 degrees of flexion with both hands.
The knees are bent in a relaxed position.

units.title: TEST POSITIONING

units.title: POSITIVE FINDING

units.title: ACTION

units.title: POSITIVE FINDING
units.summary: The recognition of one tibia resting more inferiorly than the con-tralateral side may indicate a posterior sag or instability. This may be related to the posterior cruciate ligament.

units.title: SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS/COMMENTS
units.summary: This test must be performed bilaterally. Applying a superior force to the tibia from the posterior aspect may reduce the alignment to a nor-mal resting position if it is actually found to be sagging. It is important to maintain neutral tibial rotation, otherwise a positive finding may be the result of a capsular extensibility.

units.title: ACTION

The examiner then instructs the subject to active-ly contract the quadriceps muscle group in an attempt to extend the knee while retaining hip flexion. The ipsilateral foot should remain fix-ated to the table during the attempted knee extension.

units.summary: Posterior displacement of the tibia upon the femur while the subject's quadriceps remain silent indicates a posterior instability. This may be reflective of injury to any of the following structures: posterior cruciate ligament, arcuate ligament complex, and posterior oblique ligament.

Furthermore, this subluxation is reduced once the knee extends and approaches a position of approx-imately 20 degrees of flexion. At this point, the lateral tibial plateau will return to a neutral position.

units.title: SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS/COMMENTS
units.summary: Increased anterior tibial translation is not in and of itself indicative of ACL pathology. For example, a torn PCL will allow the proximal tibia to translate posteriorly, thus producing increased anterior translation during the anterior Lachman’s test. Meniscal tear (primarily of the pos-terior horn) may also contribute to an anterior translation.

units.title: ACTION
units.summary: The examiner uses his finger to tap over the medial aspect of the ankle where the posterior tibial nerve is most superficial (Figure 11-13).

units.title: POSITIVE FINDING
units.summary: Pain or tingling that radiates along the pathway of the posterior tib-ial nerve is indicative of potential tarsal tunnel syndrome. Compression of the posterior tibial nerve in the tarsal tunnel will result in referred symptoms to the medial and plantar regions of the foot.
summary_sentences: Pain or tingling that radiates along the pathway of the posterior tib-ial nerve is indicative of potential tarsal tunnel syndrome.
Compression of the posterior tibial nerve in the tarsal tunnel will result in referred symptoms to the medial and plantar regions of the foot.

units.title: SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS/COMMENTS
units.summary: A positive test simply refers to the fact that the posterior tibial nerve has been compromised. The nerve itself could be undergoing compres-sion, as would be seen with inflammation within the tarsal tunnel, or it could be undergoing traction, as is the case with a hyperpronated foot.

units.title: TEST POSITIONING
units.summary: The subject is seated or standing with the arm at rest and the shoul-der internally rotated (Figure 12-1A).
summary_sentences: The subject is seated or standing with the arm at rest and the shoul-der internally rotated (Figure 12-1A).

units.title: ACTION
units.summary: The examiner passively forward flexes the involved arm while main-taining shoulder internal rotation (Figure 12-1B). This motion is then repeated while the examiner applies an inferior glide to the humeral head (Figure 12-1C).
summary_sentences: The examiner passively forward flexes the involved arm while main-taining shoulder internal rotation (Figure 12-1B).

units.title: POSITIVE FINDING
units.summary: The reporting of shoulder joint pain is indicative of a positive test. Pain reported during passive shoulder flexion is indicative of a possible subacromial impingement. Absence of such pain on repeated passive flexion, accompanied by an inferior glide to the humeral head, confirms structural impingement.

units.title: SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS/COMMENTS
units.summary: This test can be modified by either testing in the frontal plane or the plane of the scapula, and by placing the shoulder in external rotation to assess various components of the glenohumeral complex for impinge-ment.

units.title: TEST POSITIONING
units.summary: The subject lies relaxed and supine on the examination table with arms at side (Figure 12-2A).
summary_sentences: The subject lies relaxed and supine on the examination table with arms at side (Figure 12-2A).

units.title: ACTION
units.summary: The examiner stands at the head of the examination table and places the palm of each hand under each of the subject's scapulae (Figure 12- 2B). The subject is asked to extend one of the arms into the table force-fully while the examiner simultaneously assesses the amount of pressure felt under the scapulae. The test is repeated with the other arm.

The subject is asked to extend one of the arms into the table force-fully while the examiner simultaneously assesses the amount of pressure felt under the scapulae.
The test is repeated with the other arm.

units.title: POSITIVE FINDING
units.summary: Lack of scapula pressure felt on the contralateral testing side is indicative of a decreased effort.
summary_sentences: Lack of scapula pressure felt on the contralateral testing side is indicative of a decreased effort.

units.title: SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS/COMMENTS
units.summary: Subjects who apply forceful shoulder extension into the table will likely use the contralateral scapula for stabilization. This will be noted by the examiner. By the contrary, subjects who do not apply a true effort will tend to stabilize the central portion of the upper trunk, not applying unilateral pressure under the contralaterally tested scapula.

units.title: TEST POSITIONING
units.summary: The subject is seated with the hand in a resting position.
summary_sentences: The subject is seated with the hand in a resting position.

units.title: ACTION
units.summary: The examiner first attempts to passively extend the involved distal interphalangeal (DIP) or proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint into full extension (Figure 12-3A). The examiner then asks the subject to gently attempt to actively extend the involved DIP or PIP joint against mini-mal resistance provided by the examiner.

units.summary: Inability to actively or passively extend the involved DIP or PIP joint is considered to be a positive test. If the joint is unable to be extended both actively and passively, one must consider capsuloligamentous restrictions or acute swelling and/or pain. units.title: SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS/COMMENTS
units.summary: The examiner should only apply light resistance against active joint extension for the purposes of assessing any noticeable contraction. Moderate to maximal resistance is not encouraged as any tendon dis-ruption may become complicated with increased contractile efforts. If a tendon disruption is suspected, this test should not be repeated for demonstration, confirmation, or educational purposes beyond what is necessary for clinical diagnosis.

units.title: TEST POSITIONING
units.summary: The subject is seated with the involved forearm resting on a table with the elbow in a position of 90 degrees of flexion (Figure 12-4A).
summary_sentences: The subject is seated with the involved forearm resting on a table with the elbow in a position of 90 degrees of flexion (Figure 12-4A).

units.title: ACTION
units.summary: The examiner attempts to "shake hands" with the subject. The sub-ject is then asked to pronate the forearm (Figure 12-4B).
summary_sentences: The examiner attempts to "shake hands" with the subject.
The sub-ject is then asked to pronate the forearm (Figure 12-4B).

units.title: POSITIVE FINDING
units.summary: Pain and/or muscle weakness is considered to be a positive sign fora flexor pronator musculotendinous injury.
summary_sentences: Pain and/or muscle weakness is considered to be a positive sign fora flexor pronator musculotendinous injury.

units.title: SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS/COMMENTS
units.summary: The examiner does not need to apply much resistance while the sub-ject attempts to pronate the forearm. An acute inflammatory response will illicit a painful effort on the part of the subject.

units.title: TEST POSITIONING
units.summary: The patient is seated on a table with knees flexed to 90 degrees. The involved ankle is placed in neutral dorsiflexion/plantar flexion. The examiner stabilizes the rearfoot (subtalar joint) with one hand and grasps the forefoot with the opposite hand (Figure 12-5A).
summary_sentences: The patient is seated on a table with knees flexed to 90 degrees.
The involved ankle is placed in neutral dorsiflexion/plantar flexion.
The examiner stabilizes the rearfoot (subtalar joint) with one hand and grasps the forefoot with the opposite hand (Figure 12-5A).

units.title: ACTION
units.summary: While assuring stabilization of the subtalar joint, the examiner applies a medial rotatory force (Figure 12-5B) and a lateral rotatory force (Figure 12-5C) through the midfoot. The test is performed in order to stress the ligamentous stabilizers of the talocalcaneonavicular joint, the cuneonavicular joint, the calcaneocuboid joint, the cuboideonavicular joint, the cuneocuboid joint, the intercuneiform joint, and the tarsometatarsal joints.

units.title: POSITIVE FINDING
units.summary: Pain in the region of the midfoot is a positive finding for a midfoot sprain. The location of the pain may assist the clinician in identifying the exact location of the injury with regard to the joints of the midfoot.
summary_sentences: Pain in the region of the midfoot is a positive finding for a midfoot sprain.

units.title: SPECIAL CONSIDERATIONS/COMMENTS
units.summary: This test may also be performed with the patient in supine or long-sitting. This test should not be performed if there is obvious deformity present. Midfoot injuries are commonly found in association with lateral ankle sprains.

units.title: Chvostek's Sign
units.summary: The subject can either sit or stand. The examiner taps over the masseter muscle and parotid gland (Figure 1-1). Twitching of the facial muscles, especially the masseter, indicates positive findings for facial nerve pathology. Twitching of the facial muscles may also be a result of low calcium levels in the blood.

units.title: Loading Test
units.summary: The subject sits upright in a chair. The examiner places a cotton roll between the molars on the unin-volved side and instructs the subject to bite down forcefully. The reporting of pain on the involved side by the subject indicates a positive finding, which may be reflective of an anteriorly dislocated disk. The subject may be instructed to chew on the cotton, as opposed to forcefully biting down.

units.title: Palpation Test
units.summary: The subject sits upright in a chair. The examiner faces the subject and places his fifth digits in the sub-ject's ears. The subject is instructed to repeatedly open and close the mouth while the examiner applies pressure in an anterior direction using the pads of the fifth digits (Figures 1-2A and 1-2B). The subject's reporting of pain or discomfort during opening and closing of the mouth when pressure is applied indicates a positive test.

The examiner faces the subject and places his fifth digits in the sub-ject's ears.
The subject is instructed to repeatedly open and close the mouth while the examiner applies pressure in an anterior direction using the pads of the fifth digits (Figures 1-2A and 1-2B).

units.title: Vertebral Artery Test
units.summary: The subject lies supine, and the examiner sits with both hands sup-porting the subject's head. Slowly extend, rotate, and laterally flex the subject's cervical spine to each side. Then observe the subject for dizziness, blurred vision, nys-tagmus, slurred speech, or loss of consciousness (Figure 2-1). Each posi-tion should be held for approximately 30 seconds.

Each posi-tion should be held for approximately 30 seconds.

units.title: Foraminal Compression Test (Spurling)
units.summary: With the subject seated comfortably, the examiner rests the volar surface of both hands on top of the subject's head (Figure 2-2A). The examiner applies a downward pressure while the subject lateral-ly flexes the head. The test is repeated with the subject laterally flexing to the opposite side. Lateral flexion may be performed both actively and passively (Figure 2-2B).

The examiner applies a downward pressure while the subject lateral-ly flexes the head.
The test is repeated with the subject laterally flexing to the opposite side.
Lateral flexion may be performed both actively and passively (Figure 2-2B).

units.title: Foraminal Distraction Test
units.summary: With the subject seated, the examiner places one hand under the subject's chin and the other hand around the occiput (Figure 2-3). The examiner slowly distracts the subject's head from the trunk while the subject remains in a relaxed position. The finding is positive when existing complaints of pain decrease or disappear during the distraction. This indicates that a nerve root com-pression may exist while the subject sustains normal posture and/or positioning.

units.title: Valsalva's Maneuver
units.summary: The examiner stands next to the subject. The examiner asks the subject to take a deep breath and hold while bearing down, as if having a bowel movement. Increased pain due to increased intrathecal pressure, which may be secondary to a space-occupying lesion, herniated disk, tumor, or osteo-phyte in the cervical canal is a positive finding. Pain may be localized or referred to the corresponding dermatome.

units.title: Swallowing Test
units.summary: The examiner stands next to the subject. The examiner asks the subject to swallow. Increased pain or difficulty swallowing (dysphagia) caused by anteri-or cervical spine obstructions, such as vertebral subluxations, osteo-phyte protrusion, soft tissue swelling, or tumors in the anterior cervical spine region, is positive. Be certain the subject's head is neutral, as swallowing becomes more difficult with the neck extended.

units.title: Tinel's Sign
units.summary: The subject can sit or lie supine. The examiner gently taps the cervical area near Erb’s point. Erb's point can be found anterior to the transverse process of C6, approxi-mately 2 cm superior to the location of the clavicle (Figure 2-4). A subjective reporting of a change in sensation to the upper extrem-ity on the ipsilateral side resulting in increased pain or absent/dimin-ished sensation is positive, indicating brachial plexus pathology.

units.title: Empty Can (Supraspinatus) Test
units.summary: The subject stands with both shoulders abducted to 90 degrees, hori-zontally adducted 30 degrees, and internally rotated so the subject's thumbs face the floor (Figure 3-1). The examiner resists the subject's attempts to actively forward elevate both shoulders. Involvement of the supraspinatus muscle and/or tendon is suspected with noted weakness and/or a report of pain. Weakness of the supraspinatus muscle may be a result of suprascapu-lar nerve involvement.

Weakness of the supraspinatus muscle may be a result of suprascapu-lar nerve involvement.

units.title: Yergason Test
units.summary: The subject sits with the elbow flexed to 90 degrees and stabilized against the thorax. The forearm is in a pronated position. The examiner places one hand along the subject's forearm and the other hand on the proximal portion of the subject's humerus, near the bicipital groove (Figure 3-2A). The examiner resists the subject's attempt to actively supinate the forearm and externally rotate the humerus (Figure 3-2B).

The examiner resists the subject's attempt to actively supinate the forearm and externally rotate the humerus (Figure 3-2B).

units.title: Speed's Test
units.summary: The subject sits on a table or stands. The involved shoulder is flexed to 90 degrees, the elbow is fully extended, and the forearm is supinated. The examiner places one hand along the volar aspect of the subject's forearm and the other hand on the proximal aspect of the subject's humerus near the area of the bicipital groove (Figure 3-3). The examiner resists the subject's attempt to actively flex the humerus forward.

units.title: Ludington's Sign
units.summary: The subject sits or stands while the examiner stands directly behind the subject. The subject interlocks his fingers and places them on the superior/posterior aspect of his head. The examiner palpates the long head of the biceps tendon bilateral-ly while the subject contracts both the left and right biceps brachii mus-cles simultaneously (Figure 3-4). PosiTivVE FINDING Increased pain is indicative of a biceps brachii long head tendinitis.

units.title: Drop Arm Test
units.summary: The subject sits on a table or stands. The examiner passively abducts the subject's involved arm to 90 degrees and then instructs the subject to slowly lower the arm to the side (Figures 3-5A and 3-5B). The subject is unable to slowly return the arm to the side and/or has significant pain when attempting to perform the task. This is indicative of rotator cuff pathology.

units.title: Lateral Scapular Slide Test (LSST)
units.summary: Position 1: The subject stands with arms relaxed at the sides. Position 2: The subject stands with hands on the hips and shoulders in 10 degrees of extension. Position 3: The subject stands with shoulders abducted to 90 degrees and maximally internally rotated. Position 1: The examiner measures the distance from the inferior angle of the scapula (involved side) to the spinous process of the thoracic vertebra in the same horizontal plane (this vertebra will be used as the reference vertebra for all three positions) (Figure 3-6A).

Position 2: The subject stands with hands on the hips and shoulders in 10 degrees of extension.
Position 3: The subject stands with shoulders abducted to 90 degrees and maximally internally rotated.

units.title: Apley's Scratch Test
units.summary: The examiner stands next to the subject. The subject is instructed to take one hand and touch the opposite shoulder. Repeat with the other hand to opposite side (Figure 3-7A). The subject is then instructed to place the arm overhead and reach behind the neck as if scratching the upper back.

Repeat with the other hand to opposite side (Figure 3-7A).

units.title: Cross-Over Impingement Test
units.summary: The examiner stands with one hand on the posteri-or aspect of the subject's shoulder to stabilize the trunk and the other hand grasping the subject's elbow on the test arm. With the subject's trunk stabilized, the examiner passively and max-imally horizontally adducts the test shoulder (Figure 3-8). Superior shoulder pain is indicative of acromioclavicular joint pathology. Anterior shoulder pain is indicative of subscapularis, supraspinatus, and/or biceps long head pathology.

units.title: Posterior Impingement Test
units.summary: The subject lies supine on a table with the test shoulder placed in 90- 110 degrees of abduction and 10-15 degrees of extension. The test elbow is flexed to 90 degrees. The examiner stands with the distal hand grasping the subject's wrist and hand and the proximal hand grasping the subject's elbow (Figure 3-9A). The examiner slowly rotates the subject's shoulder into maximal external rotation (Figure 3-9B).

The examiner stands with the distal hand grasping the subject's wrist and hand and the proximal hand grasping the subject's elbow (Figure 3-9A).
The examiner slowly rotates the subject's shoulder into maximal external rotation (Figure 3-9B).

units.title: Neer Impingement Test
units.summary: With the subject's scapula stabilized, the examiner passively and maximally forward flexes the test shoulder (Figure 3-10). Shoulder pain and apprehension are indicative of shoulder impinge-ment, particularly of the supraspinatus and biceps long head tendons. A false positive test may be elicited if the subject has limited forward flexion to the extent that anatomical impingement is not the limiting factor.

units.title: Hawkins-Kennedy Impingement Test
units.summary: The subject sits or stands with both upper extremities relaxed. The examiner stands with one hand grasping the subject's elbow and the other hand grasping the subject's wrist, both on the test arm. The examiner forward flexes the shoulder to 90 degrees and then internally rotates the subject's test shoulder (Figure 3-11). Shoulder pain and apprehension are indicative of shoulder impinge-ment, particularly of the supraspinatus tendon.

units.title: Sternoclavicular (SC) Joint Stress Test
units.summary: The subject sits with the involved arm relaxed at the side. The exam-iner stands in front of the subject, placing one hand on the proximal end of the subject's clavicle and the other hand on the spine of the scapula (Figure 3-12). The examiner applies gentle inferior and posterior pressure on the clavicle, noting any movement at the sternoclavicular joint. Pain and/or movement of the clavicle indicates a sternoclavicular lig-ament sprain, possibly involving the costoclavicular ligament.

units.summary: The subject sits with the involved arm relaxed at the side and the elbow flexed to 90 degrees. The examiner stands on the involved side and with one hand holds the subject's arm just above the elbow crease. The examiner's other hand is placed over the involved acromioclavicu-lar joint (Figure 3-13). The examiner applies gentle downward pressure on the arm, noting any movement at the acromioclavicular joint.

units.title: Acromioclavicular (AC) Joint Compression Test (Shear)
units.summary: The subject sits with the involved arm relaxed at the side. The exam-iner stands on the involved side, placing one hand on the subject's clav-icle and the other hand on the spine of the scapula (Figure 3-14). The examiner gently squeezes the hands together, noting any move-ment at the acromioclavicular joint. Pain and/or movement of the clavicle is a positive indication of an acromioclavicular and/or coracoclavicular ligament sprain.

units.title: Piano Key Sign
units.summary: The subject sits with the involved limb relaxed at the side, or stands facing the examiner. The examiner applies pressure to the subject's distal clavicle in an inferior direction (Figure 3-15A). The examiner is able to use inferior pressure to depress the clavicle into its normal resting position and subsequently watch the clavicle ele-vate again once the pressure is removed (Figure 3-15B). This finding is indicative of the instability of the acromioclavicular joint on the involved side.

The examiner applies pressure to the subject's distal clavicle in an inferior direction (Figure 3-15A).
The examiner is able to use inferior pressure to depress the clavicle into its normal resting position and subsequently watch the clavicle ele-vate again once the pressure is removed (Figure 3-15B).
This finding is indicative of the instability of the acromioclavicular joint on the involved side.

units.title: Apprehension Test (Anterior)
units.summary: The subject lies supine on a table. With the subject's involved shoulder in 90 degrees of abduction and the elbow in 90 degrees of flexion, the examiner slowly externally rotates the shoulder (Figure 3-16). A positive finding for this test can be interpreted if the subject looks apprehensive or expresses feelings of apprehension toward further movement in the externally rotated direction. This test is used to mimic the positioning and movement of an anterior dislocation of the gleno-humeral joint, thus recreating a subject's episode of instability.
summary_sentences: The subject lies supine on a table.
With the subject's involved shoulder in 90 degrees of abduction and the elbow in 90 degrees of flexion, the examiner slowly externally rotates the shoulder (Figure 3-16).
A positive finding for this test can be interpreted if the subject looks apprehensive or expresses feelings of apprehension toward further movement in the externally rotated direction.
This test is used to mimic the positioning and movement of an anterior dislocation of the gleno-humeral joint, thus recreating a subject's episode of instability.

units.title: Apprehension Test (Posterior)
units.summary: The subject lies supine on a table. The examiner grasps the subject's elbow with one hand and stabilizes the ipsilateral and involved shoulder with the other hand. The examiner places the subject's involved shoulder in a position of 90 degrees of flexion and internal rotation while applying a posterior force through the long axis of the humerus (Figure 3-17). A positive finding for this test can be interpreted if the subject looks apprehensive or expresses feelings of apprehension toward further movement in the posterior direction.
summary_sentences: The subject lies supine on a table.
The examiner grasps the subject's elbow with one hand and stabilizes the ipsilateral and involved shoulder with the other hand.
The examiner places the subject's involved shoulder in a position of 90 degrees of flexion and internal rotation while applying a posterior force through the long axis of the humerus (Figure 3-17).
A positive finding for this test can be interpreted if the subject looks apprehensive or expresses feelings of apprehension toward further movement in the posterior direction.

units.title: Sulcus Sign
units.summary: The subject sits with the forearms and hands resting in the lap. The examiner stands with the proximal hand grasping the subject's scapula (superiorly) and the distal hand grasping the subject's elbow (Figure With the scapula stabilized, the examiner applies an inferior (distrac-tion) force with the distal hand. Excessive inferior humeral head translation with a visible and/or palpable “step-off’ or “sulcus” deformity immediately inferior to the acromion (laterally) is indicative of inferior and/or multidirectional instability.
summary_sentences: The subject sits with the forearms and hands resting in the lap.
The examiner stands with the proximal hand grasping the subject's scapula (superiorly) and the distal hand grasping the subject's elbow (Figure
With the scapula stabilized, the examiner applies an inferior (distrac-tion) force with the distal hand.

Excessive inferior humeral head translation with a visible and/or palpable “step-off’ or “sulcus” deformity immediately inferior to the acromion (laterally) is indicative of inferior and/or multidirectional instability.

units.title: Anterior Drawer Test
units.summary: The subject lies supine with the glenohumeral joint positioned at the edge of the table. The examiner stands next to the involved shoulder, placing one hand around the humerus below the surgical neck. The other hand stabilizes the scapula by placing the fingers behind the sub-ject on the spine of the scapula and the thumb over the coracoid process (Figure 3-19). The subject must remain relaxed while the examiner passively abducts the glenohumeral joint 70 to 80 degrees, forward flexes 0 to 10 degrees, and externally rotates 0 to 10 degrees.
summary_sentences: The subject lies supine with the glenohumeral joint positioned at the edge of the table.
The examiner stands next to the involved shoulder, placing one hand around the humerus below the surgical neck.
The other hand stabilizes the scapula by placing the fingers behind the sub-ject on the spine of the scapula and the thumb over the coracoid process (Figure 3-19).
The subject must remain relaxed while the examiner passively abducts the glenohumeral joint 70 to 80 degrees, forward flexes 0 to 10 degrees, and externally rotates 0 to 10 degrees.

units.title: Posterior Drawer Test
units.summary: The examiner stands next to the involved shoulder, holds the subject's arm at the elbow, passively abducts the shoulder to 90 degrees, and horizontally flexes the shoulder 20 to 30 degrees. The subject's elbow is flexed in a relaxed position. The exam-iner stabilizes the scapula by placing the other hand posterior to the shoulder joint capsule with the thumb over the coracoid process (Figure While stabilizing the scapula, the examiner applies downward pres-sure, pushing the humeral head posteriorly.
