The subject's elbow is flexed in a relaxed position.
The exam-iner stabilizes the scapula by placing the other hand posterior to the shoulder joint capsule with the thumb over the coracoid process (Figure
While stabilizing the scapula, the examiner applies downward pres-sure, pushing the humeral head posteriorly.

units.title: Jobe Relocation Test
units.summary: The subject lies supine with the test shoulder in 90 degrees of abduc-tion and full external rotation. The examiner stands with the distal hand grasping the subject's wrist and hand. The examiner's proximal hand is placed over the subject's humeral head (anteriorly) (Figure 3-21). The examiner applies a posterior force to the humeral head, while the examiner externally rotates the subject's humerus
summary_sentences: The subject lies supine with the test shoulder in 90 degrees of abduc-tion and full external rotation.
The examiner stands with the distal hand grasping the subject's wrist and hand.
The examiner's proximal hand is placed over the subject's humeral head (anteriorly) (Figure 3-21).
The examiner applies a posterior force to the humeral head, while the examiner externally rotates the subject's humerus

units.title: Surprise Test (Active Release Test)
units.summary: The subject lies supine with the test shoulder in 90 degrees of abduc-tion and full external rotation. The examiner stands with the distal hand grasping the subject's wrist and hand and the proximal hand placed over the subject's humeral head (anteriorly), applying a posteriorly-direct force to the humeral head (Figure 3-22A). The examiner quickly removes the proximal hand from the humeral head (Figure 3-22B). A sudden return of symptoms that were elicited from the Apprehen-sion Test is indicative of anterior instability.
summary_sentences: The subject lies supine with the test shoulder in 90 degrees of abduc-tion and full external rotation.

The examiner stands with the distal hand grasping the subject's wrist and hand and the proximal hand placed over the subject's humeral head (anteriorly), applying a posteriorly-direct force to the humeral head (Figure 3-22A).
The examiner quickly removes the proximal hand from the humeral head (Figure 3-22B).
A sudden return of symptoms that were elicited from the Apprehen-sion Test is indicative of anterior instability.

units.title: Feagin Test
units.summary: The subject stands with the involved arm abducted to 90 degrees. The elbow is extended and allowed to rest on the examiner's shoulder. The examiner stands to the side of the subject and clasps his hands together around the upper and middle thirds of the humerus. The examiner attempts to glide the humerus in an anterior and infe-rior direction (Figure 3-23).
summary_sentences: The subject stands with the involved arm abducted to 90 degrees.
The elbow is extended and allowed to rest on the examiner's shoulder.
The examiner stands to the side of the subject and clasps his hands together around the upper and middle thirds of the humerus.
The examiner attempts to glide the humerus in an anterior and infe-rior direction (Figure 3-23).

units.title: Load and Shift Test
units.summary: The subject sits with no upper trunk stabilization and the involved arm resting at the side. The examiner stands slightly behind the subject while stabilizing the clavicle and scapula with one hand. With the other hand, the examiner grasps the subject's humeral head with the thumb posterior-ly. The examiner places an axial load along the shaft of the humerus (load) in an attempt to compress the humeral head into the glenoid fossa.
summary_sentences: The subject sits with no upper trunk stabilization and the involved arm resting at the side.
The examiner stands slightly behind the subject while stabilizing the clavicle and scapula with one hand.
With the other hand, the examiner grasps the subject's humeral head with the thumb posterior-ly.
The examiner places an axial load along the shaft of the humerus (load) in an attempt to compress the humeral head into the glenoid fossa.

units.title: Grind Test
units.summary: The subject lies supine on a table with the shoulder abducted to 90 degrees and the elbow flexed to 90 degrees on the involved side. The examiner grasps the subject's elbow with one hand and the subject's proximal humerus with the other hand (Figure 3-25). The examiner applies compression to the glenoid labrum while attempting to rotate the humeral head 360 degrees around the surface of the glenoid fossa. A positive finding of a grinding or clunking sensation may be indica-tive of a glenoid labrum tear to the specific location, which is being compressed.
summary_sentences: The subject lies supine on a table with the shoulder abducted to 90 degrees and the elbow flexed to 90 degrees on the involved side.
The examiner grasps the subject's elbow with one hand and the subject's proximal humerus with the other hand (Figure 3-25).
The examiner applies compression to the glenoid labrum while attempting to rotate the humeral head 360 degrees around the surface of the glenoid fossa.
A positive finding of a grinding or clunking sensation may be indica-tive of a glenoid labrum tear to the specific location, which is being compressed.

units.title: Clunk Test
units.summary: The subject lies supine on a table. The examiner places one hand on the posterior aspect of the subject's humeral head and the other hand proximal to the subject's elbow joint along the distal humerus (Figure 3- The examiner passively abducts and externally rotates the subject's arm overhead and applies an anterior force to the humerus. (The exam-iner may also choose to internally rotate the humerus at the same time the anterior force is being applied).
summary_sentences: The subject lies supine on a table.
The examiner places one hand on the posterior aspect of the subject's humeral head and the other hand proximal to the subject's elbow joint along the distal humerus (Figure 3-
The examiner passively abducts and externally rotates the subject's arm overhead and applies an anterior force to the humerus.
(The exam-iner may also choose to internally rotate the humerus at the same time the anterior force is being applied).

units.title: Crank Test
units.summary: With the subject standing, the examiner places the distal hand on the subject's elbow and the proximal hand on the subject's proximal humerus and then passively elevates the subject's shoulder to 160 degrees in the scapular plane. With the distal hand, the examiner applies a load along the long axis of the humerus while the proximal hand externally (Figure 3-27A) and internally (Figure 3-27B) rotates the humerus. Pain and/or clicking are indicative of glenoid labral pathology. This test can also be performed in the supine position should appre-hension or muscle guarding be a concern in the standing position.
summary_sentences: With the subject standing, the examiner places the distal hand on the subject's elbow and the proximal hand on the subject's proximal humerus and then passively elevates the subject's shoulder to 160 degrees in the scapular plane.
With the distal hand, the examiner applies a load along the long axis of the humerus while the proximal hand externally (Figure 3-27A) and internally (Figure 3-27B) rotates the humerus.
Pain and/or clicking are indicative of glenoid labral pathology.
This test can also be performed in the supine position should appre-hension or muscle guarding be a concern in the standing position.

units.title: O'Brien Test (Active Compression)
units.summary: The subject sits or stands with the test shoulder in 90 degrees of for-ward flexion, 30 to 45 degrees of horizontal adduction, and maximal internal rotation. The examiner stands with one hand grasping the sub-ject's test wrist (medially) (Figure 3-28A). The subject horizontally adducts and flexes the test shoulder against the examiner's manual resistance (Figure 3-28B). The test is then repeat-ed with the subject's arm in an externally rotated position.
summary_sentences: The subject sits or stands with the test shoulder in 90 degrees of for-ward flexion, 30 to 45 degrees of horizontal adduction, and maximal internal rotation.
The examiner stands with one hand grasping the sub-ject's test wrist (medially) (Figure 3-28A).
The subject horizontally adducts and flexes the test shoulder against the examiner's manual resistance (Figure 3-28B).
The test is then repeat-ed with the subject's arm in an externally rotated position.

units.title: Brachial Plexus Stretch Test
units.summary: The examiner stands behind the subject and places one hand on the side of the subject's head and the other hand on the shoulder of the same side. The examiner laterally flexes the subject's head while applying gen-tle downward pressure on the shoulder (Figure 3-29). Pain that radiates into the subject's arm opposite to the laterally flexed neck indicates a positive finding. If pain is in the neck on the side toward lateral flexion, a pinched nerve or facet joint impingement may exist.
summary_sentences: The examiner stands behind the subject and places one hand on the side of the subject's head and the other hand on the shoulder of the same side.
The examiner laterally flexes the subject's head while applying gen-tle downward pressure on the shoulder (Figure 3-29).
Pain that radiates into the subject's arm opposite to the laterally flexed neck indicates a positive finding.
If pain is in the neck on the side toward lateral flexion, a pinched nerve or facet joint impingement may exist.

units.title: Adson's Maneuver
units.summary: The examiner stands with fingers over the radial artery (distally) (Figure 3-30A). The examiner externally rotates and extends the subject's test arm while palpating the radial pulse. The subject then extends and rotates the neck toward the test arm and takes a deep breath (Figure 3-30B). A diminished or absent radial pulse is indicative of thoracic outlet syndrome, secondary to compression of the subclavian artery by the scalene muscles.
summary_sentences: The examiner stands with fingers over the radial artery (distally) (Figure 3-30A).
The examiner externally rotates and extends the subject's test arm while palpating the radial pulse.
The subject then extends and rotates the neck toward the test arm and takes a deep breath (Figure 3-30B).
A diminished or absent radial pulse is indicative of thoracic outlet syndrome, secondary to compression of the subclavian artery by the scalene muscles.

units.title: Allen's Test
units.summary: The subject sits or stands with the test shoulder in 90 degrees of abduction and external rotation, and the elbow in 90 degrees of flexion. The examiner stands with fingers over the radial artery (distally). The subject rotates the neck away from the test arm while the exam-iner palpates the radial pulse (Figure 3-31). A diminished or absent radial pulse is indicative of thoracic outlet syndrome.
summary_sentences: The subject sits or stands with the test shoulder in 90 degrees of abduction and external rotation, and the elbow in 90 degrees of flexion.
The examiner stands with fingers over the radial artery (distally).
The subject rotates the neck away from the test arm while the exam-iner palpates the radial pulse (Figure 3-31).
A diminished or absent radial pulse is indicative of thoracic outlet syndrome.

units.title: Roos Test
units.summary: The subject sits or stands with both shoulders in 90 degrees of abduc-tion and external rotation, and the elbows in 90 degrees of flexion. The subject rapidly opens and closes both hands for 3 minutes (Figures 3-32A and 3-32B). PosiITIVE FINDING The inability to maintain the test position, diminished motor function of the hands, and/or loss of sensation in the upper extremities are indica-tive of thoracic outlet syndrome secondary to neurovascular compromise. This test evaluates both neural and vascular structures and is consid-ered to be the most accurate clinical test for assessing thoracic outlet syndrome.
summary_sentences: The subject sits or stands with both shoulders in 90 degrees of abduc-tion and external rotation, and the elbows in 90 degrees of flexion.
The subject rapidly opens and closes both hands for 3 minutes (Figures 3-32A and 3-32B).

PosiITIVE FINDING The inability to maintain the test position, diminished motor function of the hands, and/or loss of sensation in the upper extremities are indica-tive of thoracic outlet syndrome secondary to neurovascular compromise.
This test evaluates both neural and vascular structures and is consid-ered to be the most accurate clinical test for assessing thoracic outlet syndrome.

units.title: Military Brace Position
units.summary: The subject stands in the anatomical position. The examiner stands behind the subject and unilaterally assesses the radial pulse. The subject's same arm is then passively extended and abducted to 30 degrees by the examiner, while the subject simultane-ously hyperextends the head and neck (Figure 3-33). A diminished or absent radial pulse may indicate potential thoracic outlet syndrome.
summary_sentences: The subject stands in the anatomical position.
The examiner stands behind the subject and unilaterally assesses the radial pulse.
The subject's same arm is then passively extended and abducted to 30 degrees by the examiner, while the subject simultane-ously hyperextends the head and neck (Figure 3-33).
A diminished or absent radial pulse may indicate potential thoracic outlet syndrome.

units.title: Pectoralis Major Contracture Test
units.summary: The subject lies supine with both hands clasped together behind the head. The examiner stands directly behind the subject (Figure 3-34A). The examiner passively moves the subject's elbows toward the table. The subject is asked to relax the upper extremity musculature during this movement (Figure 3-348).
summary_sentences: The subject lies supine with both hands clasped together behind the head.
The examiner stands directly behind the subject (Figure 3-34A).
The examiner passively moves the subject's elbows toward the table.
The subject is asked to relax the upper extremity musculature during this movement (Figure 3-348).

units.title: Resistive Tennis Elbow Test (Cozen's Test)
units.summary: The examiner stabilizes the involved elbow while palpating along the lateral epicondyle (Figure 4-1A). With a closed fist, the subject pronates and radially deviates the fore-arm and extends the wrist against the examiner's resistance (Figure 4- A report of pain along the lateral epicondyle region of the humerus or objective muscle weakness as a result of complaints of discomfort may indicate lateral epicondylitis. REFERENCE Budoff JE, Nirschl RP.
summary_sentences: The examiner stabilizes the involved elbow while palpating along the lateral epicondyle (Figure 4-1A).
With a closed fist, the subject pronates and radially deviates the fore-arm and extends the wrist against the examiner's resistance (Figure 4-
A report of pain along the lateral epicondyle region of the humerus or objective muscle weakness as a result of complaints of discomfort may indicate lateral epicondylitis.
REFERENCE Budoff JE, Nirschl RP.

units.title: Resistive Tennis Elbow Test
units.summary: The examiner stabilizes the involved elbow with one hand and places the palm of the other hand on the dorsal aspect of the subject's hand just distal to the proximal interphalangeal joint of the third digit (Figure 4-2). The subject extends the third digit against the examiner's resistance. A reporting of pain along the lateral epicondyle region of the humerus or objective muscle weakness as a result of complaints of dis-comfort may indicate lateral epicondylitis. Clinicians have reported differentiating between the extensor carpi radialis longus (resistance over the second metacarpal) and the extensor carpi radialis brevis (resistance over the third metacarpal).
summary_sentences: The examiner stabilizes the involved elbow with one hand and places the palm of the other hand on the dorsal aspect of the subject's hand just distal to the proximal interphalangeal joint of the third digit (Figure 4-2).
The subject extends the third digit against the examiner's resistance.
A reporting of pain along the lateral epicondyle region of the humerus or objective muscle weakness as a result of complaints of dis-comfort may indicate lateral epicondylitis.

Clinicians have reported differentiating between the extensor carpi radialis longus (resistance over the second metacarpal) and the extensor carpi radialis brevis (resistance over the third metacarpal).

units.title: Passive Tennis Elbow Test
units.summary: The subject sits with the involved elbow in full extension. The examiner passively pronates the forearm and flexes the subject's wrist (Figure 4-3A). A reporting of pain along the lateral epicondyle region of the humerus may indicate lateral epicondylitis. The examiner may also palpate the involved lateral epicondyle region during the test to assess the tightness of the common extensor tendon origin.
summary_sentences: The subject sits with the involved elbow in full extension.
The examiner passively pronates the forearm and flexes the subject's wrist (Figure 4-3A).
A reporting of pain along the lateral epicondyle region of the humerus may indicate lateral epicondylitis.
The examiner may also palpate the involved lateral epicondyle region during the test to assess the tightness of the common extensor tendon origin.

units.title: Golfer's Elbow Test
units.summary: The subject sits or stands and makes a fist on the involved side. The examiner faces the subject and palpates along the medial epicondyle. The examiner's other hand grasps the subject's wrist (Figure 4-4A). The examiner passively supinates the forearm and extends the elbow and wrist (Figure 4-4B).
summary_sentences: The subject sits or stands and makes a fist on the involved side.
The examiner faces the subject and palpates along the medial epicondyle.
The examiner's other hand grasps the subject's wrist (Figure 4-4A).
The examiner passively supinates the forearm and extends the elbow and wrist (Figure 4-4B).

units.title: Hyperextension Test
units.summary: The subject sits or stands with the elbow fully extended and the fore-arm supinated. The examiner grasps the distal humerus at the areas of the medial and lateral epicondyles with one hand, while the other hand grasps the distal forearm of the subject (Figure 4-5). The examiner passively extends the elbow until no further motion is available. Elbow extension beyond 0 degrees is considered hyperextension.
summary_sentences: The subject sits or stands with the elbow fully extended and the fore-arm supinated.
The examiner grasps the distal humerus at the areas of the medial and lateral epicondyles with one hand, while the other hand grasps the distal forearm of the subject (Figure 4-5).
The examiner passively extends the elbow until no further motion is available.
Elbow extension beyond 0 degrees is considered hyperextension.

units.title: Elbow Flexion Test
units.summary: The examiner stands next to the subject. The subject is instructed to maximally flex the elbow and hold this position for 3 to 5 minutes (Figure 4-6). Radiating pain into the median nerve distribution in the subject's arm and/or hand (ie, lateral forearm or tip of thumb, index and middle fin-ger, lateral half of index finger) is a positive finding. A positive test is indicative of cubital fossa syndrome.
summary_sentences: The examiner stands next to the subject.
The subject is instructed to maximally flex the elbow and hold this position for 3 to 5 minutes (Figure 4-6).
Radiating pain into the median nerve distribution in the subject's arm and/or hand (ie, lateral forearm or tip of thumb, index and middle fin-ger, lateral half of index finger) is a positive finding.
A positive test is indicative of cubital fossa syndrome.

units.title: Varus Stress Test
units.summary: The subject sits with the test elbow flexed to 20 to 30 degrees. The examiner stands with the distal hand around subject's wrist (laterally) and the proximal hand over the subject's elbow joint (medially) (Figure With the wrist stabilized, the examiner applies a varus stress to the elbow with the proximal hand. As compared to the uninvolved elbow, lateral elbow pain and/or increased varus movement with a diminished or absent endpoint is indicative of damage to primarily the radial (lateral) collateral ligament.
summary_sentences: The subject sits with the test elbow flexed to 20 to 30 degrees.
The examiner stands with the distal hand around subject's wrist (laterally) and the proximal hand over the subject's elbow joint (medially) (Figure
With the wrist stabilized, the examiner applies a varus stress to the elbow with the proximal hand.

As compared to the uninvolved elbow, lateral elbow pain and/or increased varus movement with a diminished or absent endpoint is indicative of damage to primarily the radial (lateral) collateral ligament.

units.title: Valgus Stress Test
units.summary: The subject sits with the test elbow flexed to 20 to 30 degrees. The examiner stands with the distal hand around the subject's wrist (medial-ly) and the proximal hand over the subject's elbow joint (laterally) (Figure 4-8). With the wrist stabilized, the examiner applies a valgus stress to the elbow with the proximal hand. As compared to the uninvolved elbow, medial elbow and/or increased valgus movement with a diminished or absent endpoint is indicative of damage to primarily the ulnar (medial) collateral ligament.
summary_sentences: The subject sits with the test elbow flexed to 20 to 30 degrees.
The examiner stands with the distal hand around the subject's wrist (medial-ly) and the proximal hand over the subject's elbow joint (laterally) (Figure 4-8).
With the wrist stabilized, the examiner applies a valgus stress to the elbow with the proximal hand.
As compared to the uninvolved elbow, medial elbow and/or increased valgus movement with a diminished or absent endpoint is indicative of damage to primarily the ulnar (medial) collateral ligament.

units.title: Tinel's Sign
units.summary: The subject is seated with the elbow in slight flexion, and the examin-er is standing with the distal hand grasping the subject's wrist (laterally). With the wrist stabilized, tap the ulnar nerve in the ulnar notch (between the olecranon process and medial epicondyle) with the index finger (Figure 4-9). Tingling along the ulnar distribution of the forearm, hand, and fin-gers is indicative of ulnar nerve compromise. A positive finding can be related to traction of the ulnar nerve from a valgus force or it can be related to some type of compression of the nerve itself, as would be seen with inflammation surrounding the area.
summary_sentences: The subject is seated with the elbow in slight flexion, and the examin-er is standing with the distal hand grasping the subject's wrist (laterally).
With the wrist stabilized, tap the ulnar nerve in the ulnar notch (between the olecranon process and medial epicondyle) with the index finger (Figure 4-9).
Tingling along the ulnar distribution of the forearm, hand, and fin-gers is indicative of ulnar nerve compromise.

A positive finding can be related to traction of the ulnar nerve from a valgus force or it can be related to some type of compression of the nerve itself, as would be seen with inflammation surrounding the area.

units.title: Pinch Grip Test
units.summary: The examiner stands next to the subject. The subject is instructed to pinch the tips of the thumb and index finger together (Figure 4-10). The inability to touch the tips of the thumb and index finger togeth-er demonstrates a positive finding. Touching the pads of the thumb and index finger indicates pathology of the anterior interosseous nerve between the two heads of the pronator muscle.
summary_sentences: The examiner stands next to the subject.
The subject is instructed to pinch the tips of the thumb and index finger together (Figure 4-10).
The inability to touch the tips of the thumb and index finger togeth-er demonstrates a positive finding.
Touching the pads of the thumb and index finger indicates pathology of the anterior interosseous nerve between the two heads of the pronator muscle.

units.title: Tap or Percussion Test
units.summary: The subject may sit or stand with the affected finger extended. The examiner stands in front of the subject. The examiner applies a firm tap to the end of the finger being tested (Figures 5-1A). As an alternative method to tapping, the examiner may use a percussion hammer (Figure 5-1B).
summary_sentences: The subject may sit or stand with the affected finger extended.
The examiner stands in front of the subject.
The examiner applies a firm tap to the end of the finger being tested (Figures 5-1A).
As an alternative method to tapping, the examiner may use a percussion hammer (Figure 5-1B).

units.title: Compression Test
units.summary: The subject may sit or stand with the affected finger extended. The examiner stands in front of the subject. The examiner holds the distal phalanx and applies compression along the long axis of the bone of the finger being tested (Figure 5-2). Pain at the site of injury indicates a fracture.
summary_sentences: The subject may sit or stand with the affected finger extended.
The examiner stands in front of the subject.
The examiner holds the distal phalanx and applies compression along the long axis of the bone of the finger being tested (Figure 5-2).
Pain at the site of injury indicates a fracture.

units.title: Long Finger Flexion Test
units.summary: The examiner stands in front of the subject and holds the sub-ject’s fingers in extension, except for the finger being tested. The examiner isolates the distal interphalangeal joint by stabiliz-ing the metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints of the finger being tested. The subject is instructed to flex the finger being tested at the dis-tal interphalangeal joint (Figure 5-3A). The examiner isolates the proximal interphalangeal joint by sta-bilizing the metacarpophalangeal joint.
summary_sentences: The examiner stands in front of the subject and holds the sub-ject’s fingers in extension, except for the finger being tested.
The examiner isolates the distal interphalangeal joint by stabiliz-ing the metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints of the finger being tested.
The subject is instructed to flex the finger being tested at the dis-tal interphalangeal joint (Figure 5-3A).
The examiner isolates the proximal interphalangeal joint by sta-bilizing the metacarpophalangeal joint.

units.title: Finkelstein Test
units.summary: The subject sits or stands and forms a fist around the thumb. The examiner stands with the proximal hand grasping the subject's forearm and the distal hand grasping the subject's fist, with the subject's thumb in the examiner's thenar eminence. While stabilizing the subject's forearm with the proximal hand, ulnarly deviate the subject's wrist with the distal hand (Figure 5-4A). Pain over the abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis tendons distally is indicative of tenosynovitis in these tendons (de Quervain’'s disease).
summary_sentences: The subject sits or stands and forms a fist around the thumb.
The examiner stands with the proximal hand grasping the subject's forearm and the distal hand grasping the subject's fist, with the subject's thumb in the examiner's thenar eminence.
While stabilizing the subject's forearm with the proximal hand, ulnarly deviate the subject's wrist with the distal hand (Figure 5-4A).
Pain over the abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis tendons distally is indicative of tenosynovitis in these tendons (de Quervain’'s disease).

units.title: Phalen Test
units.summary: The subject sits or stands with the dorsal aspect of both hands in full contact so that both wrists are maximally flexed (Figure 5-5). A steady compressive force is applied through the subject's forearms so that the subject's wrists are maximally flexed for 1 minute. Numbness and tingling in the median nerve distribution of the fin-gers (ie, thumb, index finger, middle finger, and lateral aspect of the ring finger) are indicative of carpal tunnel syndrome secondary to medi-an nerve compression. Pain in the wrist area, without complaints of radiating pain distally toward the hand and fingers, may be indicative of carpal bone pathology.
summary_sentences: The subject sits or stands with the dorsal aspect of both hands in full contact so that both wrists are maximally flexed (Figure 5-5).
A steady compressive force is applied through the subject's forearms so that the subject's wrists are maximally flexed for 1 minute.

Numbness and tingling in the median nerve distribution of the fin-gers (ie, thumb, index finger, middle finger, and lateral aspect of the ring finger) are indicative of carpal tunnel syndrome secondary to medi-an nerve compression.
Pain in the wrist area, without complaints of radiating pain distally toward the hand and fingers, may be indicative of carpal bone pathology.

units.title: Tinel's Sign
units.summary: The subject sits next to a flat surface. The examiner taps the volar aspect of the subject's wrist over the area of the carpal tunnel (Figures 5-7A and 5-7B). Complaints of tingling, paresthesia, or pain by the subject in the area of the thumb, index finger, middle finger, and radial one-half of the ring finger signal a positive test. This may be indicative of a compression of the median nerve in the carpal tunnel, or carpal tunnel syndrome.

units.title: Wrinkle Test
units.summary: The subject's fingers are placed in warm water for approximately 10 minutes (Figure 5-9). Upon removal, the examiner assesses the skin around the pulp area for any wrinkling. A positive test is seen when the involved finger shows no signs of wrinkling, indicating denervated tissue. This test can be used as an assessment tool for documenting periph-eral nerve regeneration by way of pulp area wrinkling.

units.title: Digital Allen's Test
units.summary: Both the subject and examiner may sit or stand. The subject is instructed to make a fist several times in succession in order to “pump” the blood out of the hand and fingers. The subject is then instructed to maintain a fist while the examiner compresses the radi-al artery with the thumb and the ulnar artery with the fingers (Figure 5- 10A). As the subject relaxes the hand (Figure 5-10B), the examiner releas-es pressure from one artery at a time and observes the color of the hand and fingers (Figure 5-10C).

units.title: Bunnel Littler Test
units.summary: The subject sits with the metacarpophalangeal joint of the involved digit in slight extension. The examiner then passively flexes the metacar-pophalangeal joint slightly, and again assesses the amount of flexion at the proximal interphalangeal joint (Figure 5-11B). A positive finding is revealed if the proximal interphalangeal joint does not flex while the metacarpophalangeal joint is in an extended position.

units.summary: The examiner uses one hand to stabilize the distal forearm at the distal radial ulnar joint while grasping the scaphoid bone of the subject with the other hand (Figure 5-13A). The examiner mobilizes the scaphoid bone anteriorly and posterior-ly while ulnarly and radially deviating the subject's wrist (Figure 5-13B). units.title: Valgus Stress Test
units.summary: The examiner maintains stabilization of the proximal bone between the thumb and forefinger, and grasps the distal bone (usually the bones comprising a hinge joint). The examiner provides a valgus force to the joint, creating a fulcrum while attempting to “gap the joint” (Figure 5-14A). Any excessive gapping that is noted when compared to the unin-volved side may indicate a collateral ligament tear. The examiner should perform this test with extreme care so no fur-ther damage is created with the valgus stress that is applied.

Pain with compression or release of pressure indicates the possibility of a rib fracture, rib contusion, or costochondral separation.

units.summary: The examiner stands next to the sub-jeGu: The subject is instructed to breathe in and out normally, then take a deep breath followed by rapid expiration. units.title: Valsalva's Maneuver
units.summary: The examiner stands next to the subject. The examiner asks the subject to take a deep breath and hold while bearing down, as if having a bowel movement. Increased pain due to increased intrathecal pressure, which may be secondary to a space-occupying lesion, herniated disk, tumor, or osteo-phyte in the cervical canal is a positive finding. Pain may be localized or referred to the corresponding dermatome.

units.title: Stoop Test
units.summary: The subject is asked to walk briskly for a period of 1 minute. The examiner assesses for the onset of pain in the buttocks and lower limb areas. If present, the subject forward flexes the trunk (Figure 7-1). Pain in the buttocks and lower limb areas brought on by brisk walk-ing that is soon relieved with forward flexing of the trunk is an indica-tion that there is a relationship between the neurogenic intermittent claudication, posture, and walking.

A positive finding is also noted when the examiner does not feel increased pressure in the palm that underlies the resting leg.

units.title: 90-90 Straight Leg Raise Test
units.summary: The patient is instructed to actively extend one knee at a time as much as possible (Figure 7-4B). If the knee is flexed greater than 20 degrees, the hamstrings are con-sidered tight. When assessing this test, care should always be taken to be consis-tent with the position of the pelvis so that testing measures can be repeated with reliability.

units.title: Bowstring Test (Cram Test)
units.summary: The examiner performs a passive straight leg raise on the involved side (Figure 7-5A). If the subject reports radiating pain with the straight leg raise, the examiner then flexes the subject's knee to approximately 20 degrees in an attempt to reduce painful symptoms. The examiner then applies pressure to the popliteal area in an attempt to reproduce the radicular pain (Figure 7-5B). Painful radicular reproduction following popliteal compression indi-cates tension on the sciatic nerve.

units.title: Sitting Root Test
units.summary: The subject sits with the hip flexed to 90 degrees and the cervical spine in flexion. The subject actively extends the knee (Figure 7-6A). The subject who arches backward and/or complains of pain in the regions of the buttocks, posterior thigh, and calf during knee extension demonstrates a positive finding for possible sciatic nerve pain. This test can be reproduced with the examiner passively extending the subject's knee.

units.title: Unilateral Straight Leg Raise Test (Lasegue Test)
section_path: Unilateral Straight Leg Raise Test (Lasegue Test)
units.summary: The subject is supine with both hips and knees extended. The exam-iner is standing with the distal hand around the subject's heel and the proximal hand on the subject's distal thigh (anteriorly) to maintain knee extension. With the subject completely relaxed, the examiner slowly raises the test leg until pain or tightness is noted (Figure 7-7). The examiner slow-ly lowers the leg until the pain or tightness resolves, then dorsiflexes the ankle and instructs the subject to flex the neck.

units.title: Bilateral Straight Leg Raise Test
units.summary: The subject lies supine with both hips and knees extended. The examiner is standing with the distal hand or forearm around or under the subject's heels and the proximal hand on the subject's distal thighs (anteriorly) to maintain knee extension. With the subject completely relaxed, slowly raise the legs until pain or tightness is noted (Figure 7-8). Low back pain occurring at hip flexion angles less than 70 degrees is indicative of sacroiliac joint involvement.

units.title: Well Straight Leg Raise Test
units.summary: The subject lies supine on a table. The examiner places one hand on the anterior aspect of the uninvolved leg slightly superior to the knee and the other hand around the heel of the ipsilateral calcaneus. The examiner passively flexes the subject's uninvolved hip while maintaining the knee in an extended position (Figure 7-9). Complaints of pain on the involved side indicate a positive test and may be related to vertebral disk damage.

units.title: Slump Test
units.summary: The subject sits on the end of the table and leans forward while the examiner holds the head and chin upright (Figure 7-10A). Any symptomatic changes reported by the subject are noted. The examiner then flexes the subject's neck and assesses for any changes in symptoms (Figure 7-10B). If no changes are noted, the examiner pas-sively extends one of the subject's knees (Figure 7-10C).

units.title: Thomas Test
units.summary: The subject lies supine with both knees fully flexed against the chest and the buttocks near the table edge. The examiner stands with one hand on the subject's lumbar spine or iliac crest to monitor lumbar lordosis or pelvic tilt, respectively (Figure 7-11A). The subject slowly lowers the test leg until the leg is fully relaxed or until either anterior pelvic tilting or an increase in lumbar lordosis occurs (Figure 7-11B). A lack of hip extension with knee flexion greater than 45 degrees is indicative of iliopsoas muscle tightness.

units.title: Spring Test
units.summary: The subject lies prone and the examiner stands with the thumb (Figure 7-12A) or hypothenar eminence (specifically the pisiform) over the spinous process of a lumbar vertebra (Figure 7-12B). Apply a downward “springing” force through the spinous process of each vertebra to assess posterior-anterior motion. This action should be repeated for each transverse process to assess rotary motion. Increases or decreases in motion at one vertebra compared to anoth-er are indicative of hypermobility or hypomobility, respectively.

units.title: Trendelenburg's Test
units.summary: The subject stands on one lower extremity (Figures 7-13A and 7-13B). The subject remains in this position for approximately 10 seconds and then switches extremities. A positive finding is seen when the pelvis on the unsupported side drops noticeably lower than the pelvis on the supported side. This indi-cates a weakness of the gluteus medius muscle on the supported side.

units.title: Sacroiliac (SI) Joint Fixation Test

The examiner may then leave the one thumb over the sacral spinous process and move the other thumb to the ischial tuberosity. The examiner should note whether the posterior superior iliac spines are level.

units.title: Gillet Test
units.summary: The subject stands while the examiner palpates the posterior superi-or iliac spine bilaterally. The subject flexes one hip and brings the knee to the chest while the examiner maintains palpation to each PSIS and assesses overall sacroili-ac movement (Figure 8-2A). A positive sign is noted if the PSIS on the ipsilateral side of the knee being flexed does not move or moves minimally in the inferior direction (Figure 8-2B). The PSIS on the side of the hip being flexed should move slightly anteriorly during active hip flexion.

The examiner applies outward and downward pressure with the heel of the hands.

units.title: Squish Test
units.summary: The examiner compresses downward and inward at a 45-degree angle along the iliac crest and anterior superior iliac spine bilaterally. Subjective complaints of pain are noted as positive findings and may be found anteriorly or posteriorly. This test assesses the stability of the posterior sacroiliac ligaments but also directly applies compressive forces to the anterior sacroiliac joint. Thus, the location of pain should be noted and correlated with any additional findings.

units.title: Yeoman's Test
units.summary: The subject lies prone on the table. The examiner passively flexes the subject's knee to 90 degrees while simultaneously extending the ipsilateral hip (Figure 8-5A). A reporting of pain during this test is considered to be a positive sign. Pain in the sacroiliac joint may be related to anterior sacroiliac ligament pathology.

units.title: Gaenslen's Test
units.summary: The subject lies on the side of the uninvolved leg (lower leg). With the involved leg (upper leg) in slight hyperextension, the subject then flexes the knee of the uninvolved side toward the chest. The examiner stabilizes the subject's pelvis and further extends the subject's involved leg (Figure 8-6). Pain in the sacroiliac region is considered a positive finding and may be associated with sacroiliac joint dysfunction.

units.title: Patrick or FABER Test
units.summary: The subject lies supine on the table. The examiner passively flexes, abducts, and externally rotates the involved leg until the foot rests on the top of the knee of the nonin-volved lower extremity (Figure 8-7A). The examiner then slowly abducts the involved lower extremity, bringing the knee closer toward the table (Figure 8-7B). A positive finding is revealed when the involved lower extremity does not abduct below the level of the noninvolved lower extremity.

units.title: Long-Sitting Test
units.summary: The subject lies supine with both hips and knees extended, and the examiner stands with the thumbs on the subject's medial malleoli (Figure 8-8A). The examiner passively flexes both knees and hips (Figure 8-8B) and then fully extends and compares the position of the medial malleoli rel-ative to each other (Figure 8-8C). The subject then slowly assumes the long-sitting position, and malleolar position is re-assessed (Figure 8-8D). A leg that appears longer in supine position but shorter in long-sit-ting is indicative of an ipsilateral anteriorly rotated ilium.
summary_sentences: The subject lies supine with both hips and knees extended, and the examiner stands with the thumbs on the subject's medial malleoli (Figure 8-8A).
The examiner passively flexes both knees and hips (Figure 8-8B) and then fully extends and compares the position of the medial malleoli rel-ative to each other (Figure 8-8C).
The subject then slowly assumes the long-sitting position, and malleolar position is re-assessed (Figure 8-8D).
A leg that appears longer in supine position but shorter in long-sit-ting is indicative of an ipsilateral anteriorly rotated ilium.

units.title: Hip Scouring/Quadrant Test
units.summary: The examiner stands on the involved side and passively flexes and adducts the subject's hip. The subject's knee is also placed in full flexion (Figure 9-1A). The examiner applies downward pressure along the shaft of the femur while simultaneously adducting and externally rotating the hip (Figure 9-1B). The examiner then adducts and internally rotates the hip while maintaining downward pressure (Figure 9-1C).

The examiner then adducts and internally rotates the hip while maintaining downward pressure (Figure 9-1C).

units.title: Craig's Test
units.summary: The subject is lying prone with the affected leg’s knee flexed to 90 degrees. The examiner stands on the involved side and palpates the greater trochanter (Figure 9-2A). The examiner then passively internally and externally rotates the femur until the greater trochanter is parallel with the examining table (Figure 9-2B). At this point, the subject is asked to hold the hip in this position while the examiner measures the angle between the long axis of the lower leg and the perpendicular axis to the table with a goniome-ter (Figure 9-2C).

units.title: 90-90 Straight Leg Raise Test
units.summary: Test subject lies supine, stabilizing both hips at 90 degrees of flexion with both hands. The knees are bent in a relaxed position. The examin-er stands next to the subject (Figure 9-3A). The subject is instructed to actively extend one knee at a time as much as possible (Figure 9-3B).

units.title: Patrick or FABER Test
units.summary: The subject lies supine on the table. The subject flexes, abducts, and externally rotates the involved leg until the foot rests on top of the knee of the noninvolved lower extrem-ity (Figure 9-4A). The examiner then slowly abducts the involved lower extremity, bringing the knee closer toward the table (Figure 9-4B). Posirive FINDING A positive finding is revealed when the involved lower extremity does not abduct below the level of the noninvolved lower extremity.

units.title: Trendelenburg's Test
units.summary: The subject stands on one lower extremity (Figures 9-5A and 9-5B). The subject remains in this position for approximately 10 seconds and then switches extremities. A positive finding is seen when the pelvis on the unsupported side drops noticeably lower than the pelvis on the supported side. This indi-cates a weakness of the gluteus medius muscle on the supported side.

units.title: Ober's Test
units.summary: The subject lies on the side with the hips and knees extended such that the test leg is superior to the nontest leg. The examiner stands with the proximal hand stabilizing the pelvis and the distal hand supporting the lower leg (Figure 9-6A). With the pelvis stabilized to prevent rolling, abduct and extend the test hip in order to position the iliotibial band (ITB) behind the greater trochanter (Figure 9-6B). Then allow the leg to slowly lower (adduct).

units.title: Piriformis Test
units.summary: The subject lies on the nontest side with the test leg in 60 degrees of hip flexion and relaxed knee flexion. The examiner stands with the proximal hand on the subject's pelvis (laterally) and the distal hand on the subject's knee (laterally) (Figure 9-7). With the subject's pelvis stabilized, apply an adduction (downward) force on the subject's knee. Tightness or pain in the hip and buttock areas is indicative of piri-formis tightness.

units.title: Thomas Test
units.summary: The subject lies supine with both knees fully flexed against the chest and the buttocks near the table edge. The examiner stands with one hand on the subject's lumbar spine or iliac crest to monitor lumbar lor-dosis or pelvic tilt, respectively (Figure 9-8A). The subject slowly lowers the test leg until the leg is fully relaxed, or until either anterior pelvic tilting or an increase in lumbar lordosis occurs (Figure 9-8B). A lack of hip extension with knee flexion greater than 45 degrees is indicative of iliopsoas muscle tightness.

units.title: True Leg-Length Discrepancy Test
units.summary: The subject lies supine with hips and knees extended and parallel. Each leg should be perpendicular to a straight line between both ante-rior superior iliac spines. With a tape measure, the examiner measures from the most distal point of the anterior superior iliac spines to the most distal point of the medial malleolus (Figure 9-9). A difference of more than 1 cm is indicative of discrepancies in either the length of the femur or tibia, or in the angle of femoral neck inclina-tion (ie, coxa vara or valga).

units.title: Apparent Leg-Length Discrepancy Test

With a tape measure, the examiner measures from the umbilicus to the most distal point of the medial malleolus (Figure 9-10). A difference of more than 1 cm is indicative of abnormal pelvic posi-tioning.

units.title: Ely's Test

The examiner passively flexes the subject's knee and notes the reac-tion at the hip joint. This test is repeated on the other side for compar-ison (Figure 9-11A). If the hip also flexes when the knee is flexed, a tight rectus femoris is indicated (Figure 9-11B).

units.title: Patella Tendon/Patella Ligament Length Test
units.summary: The subject lies supine on a table. The examiner measures the distance between the superior pole of the patella to the inferior pole of the patella. The examiner next measures the distance between the inferior pole of the patella and the tibial tuber-cle (Figures 10-1A and 10-1B). A ratio is taken between the first and second measurements.

units.title: Patellar Apprehension Test
units.summary: The subject lies supine with both knees fully extended. The examin-er stands opposite the involved side and places both thumbs on the medial border of the patella being tested (Figure 10-2A). The subject must remain relaxed with no quadriceps contraction, while the examiner gently pushes the patella laterally. If the subject is apprehensive to this movement or contracts the quadriceps muscle to protect against subluxation, the test is indicative of patellar subluxation or dislocation (possibly due to laxity of the medi-al retinaculum).

units.title: Ballotable Patella or Patella Tap Test
section_path: Ballotable Patella or Patella Tap Test
units.summary: The subject lies supine with both knees fully extended. The examiner stands with the proximal hand over the suprapatellar pouch and the distal hand (thumb or first two fingers) over the patella (Figure 10-3). Compress the suprapatellar pouch with the proximal hand, then com-press the patella into the femur. Downward movement of the patella followed by a rebound will give the appearance of a floating or ballotable patella and is indicative of mod-erate to severe joint effusion.

units.summary: The subject lies supine with the involved knee in full extension. The examiner places both hands on the medial aspect of the patella. The examiner attempts to “milk” or “sweep” any intracapsular swelling by applying pressure to the proximal (Figure 10-4A), distal (Figure 10-4B), and lateral (Figure 10-4C) aspects of the patella. Fluid that accumulates on the medial aspect of the patella is repre-sentative of intracapsular swelling.

Place a goniometer on the knee such that the axis is over the midpoint of the patella, the proximal arm is over the line to the ante-rior superior iliac spines, and the distal arm is over the line to the tibial tubercle.

The examiner passively flexes the subject's hip and knee maximally (Figure 10-6B) and then applies a circular motion with the tibia, rotat-ing the tibia clockwise and counter-clockwise (Figure 10-6C). Pain, grinding, or clicking is indicative of a meniscal tear.

The examiner stands on the involved side and places the heel of one hand over the lateral border of the patella, with the fingers of that hand positioned over the medial femoral condyle. The ipsilateral foot should remain fix-ated to the table during the attempted knee extension.

From a “neutral” (anterior-posterior) position, apply an anterior force to the tibia with the distal hand while stabilizing the femur with the prox-imal hand.

units.summary: The subject lies supine with the test hip flexed to 45 degrees, knee flexed to 90 degrees, and tibia externally rotated 20 to 30 degrees. The examiner sits on the subject's foot with both hands behind the subject's proximal tibia and thumbs on the tibial plateau (Figure 10-23). Apply a posterior force to the proximal tibia. Increased posterior tibial displacement, particularly of the lateral tib-ial condyle, as compared to the uninvolved side is indicative of pos-terolateral rotary instability (secondary to damage of the PCL, LCL, posterolateral capsule, and arcuate complex).

units.title: Posterior Lachman's Test
units.summary: The subject lies supine with the test knee flexed to 20 to 30 degrees. The examiner stands with the proximal hand on the subject's distal thigh (laterally) immediately proximal to the patella and the distal hand on the subject's proximal tibia (medially) immediately distal to the tib-ial tubercle (Figure 10-24). From a “neutral” (anterior-posterior) position, apply a posterior force to the tibia with the distal hand while the femur is stabilized with the proximal hand. Excessive posterior translation of the tibia (as compared to the unin-volved knee) from the neutral position with a diminished or absent end-point is indicative of a partial or complete tear of the posterior cruciate ligament.

units.summary: The examiner stands and grasps a great toe with each hand. Lift both legs off the table (vertically) by the great toes (Figure 10- An increase in hyperextension and external tibial rotation as com-pared to the uninvolved knee is indicative of posterolateral rotary insta-bility (secondary to damage of primarily the PCL, LCL, posterolateral capsule, and arcuate complex). It is important for the examiner to recognize that a positive finding may not be indicative of any pathology and instead may simply be rep-resentative of one's normal joint extensibility.

units.title: Dial Test (Tibial External Rotation Test)
units.summary: The subject lies supine with the test knee in 30 degrees flexion and the ankle in neutral plantarflexion/dorsiflexion and inversion/eversion. The examiner grasps the subject's distal thigh (posteriorly) with the proximal hand and the subject's ankle from the plantar surface with the distal hand (Figure 10-26A). With the proximal hand stabilizing the subject's distal thigh, the examiner maximally externally rotates the subject's lower leg (maintain-ing the ankle in a neutral position) and measures the amount of external rotation created between the knee and medial border of the foot (Figure The test is repeated with the knee in 90 degrees of flexion (Figures 10-26C and 10-26D). An increase of >10 degrees of external rotation (as compared to the contralateral leg) at 30 degrees but not at 90 degrees is indicative of an isolated posterolateral corner injury.

units.title: Valgus Stress Test
units.summary: The subject lies supine with the knee in full extension (Figure 10- 27A). The examiner stands with the distal hand on the subject's medial ankle and the proximal hand on the knee (laterally). With the ankle stabilized, apply a valgus force at the knee with the proximal hand. This is performed with the knee in full extension and repeated with the knee in 20 to 30 degrees of flexion (Figure 10-27B).

The examiner stands with the distal hand on the subject's lateral ankle and the proximal hand on the knee (medially). units.title: McMurray Test
units.summary: The examiner stands with the distal hand grasping the subject's heel or distal leg (medially), and the proximal hand on the subject's knee with the fingers palpating the medial and lat-eral joint lines (Figure 10-29A). With the knee fully flexed (marked #1 in Figure 10-29B), externally rotate the tibia (marked #2 in Figure 10-29B), introduce a valgus force, and extend the knee (medial meniscus) (marked #3 in Figure 10-29B). Repeat with the tibia internally rotated and a varus force applied to the knee (lateral meniscus) (Figure 10-29C). A "click" along the medial joint line is indicative of a medial menis-cus tear.
summary_sentences: The examiner stands with the distal hand grasping the subject's heel or distal leg (medially), and the proximal hand on the subject's knee with the fingers palpating the medial and lat-eral joint lines (Figure 10-29A).

A "click" along the medial joint line is indicative of a medial menis-cus tear.

units.title: Apley Compression Test
units.summary: The subject lies prone with the test knee flexed to 90 degrees. The examiner stands with the proximal hand on the subject's distal thigh for stabilization and the distal hand on the subject's heel (Figure 10-30A). With the distal hand, medially and laterally rotate the tibia while applying a downward force through the heel. Pain, clicking, and/or restriction is indicative of either a medial or lat-eral meniscus tear, depending on the location of symptoms.
summary_sentences: The subject lies prone with the test knee flexed to 90 degrees.
The examiner stands with the proximal hand on the subject's distal thigh for stabilization and the distal hand on the subject's heel (Figure 10-30A).
With the distal hand, medially and laterally rotate the tibia while applying a downward force through the heel.
Pain, clicking, and/or restriction is indicative of either a medial or lat-eral meniscus tear, depending on the location of symptoms.

units.title: Steinman's Tenderness Displacement Test
units.summary: The subject lies supine with the knee in full extension. The examin-er places the proximal hand under the involved knee and grasps the ankle with the distal hand (Figure 10-31A). The examiner passively moves the subject's involved knee into vari-ous ranges of knee flexion, followed by a dynamic movement into inter-nal rotation (Figure 10-31B) and external rotation (Figure 10-31C). A subject who either complains of pain during the rotational com-ponent or lacks full flexion may have a meniscal tear.

units.title: Homans' Sign
units.summary: The subject lies supine on a table. With the knee of the involved side fully extended, the examiner pas-sively dorsiflexes the subject's foot (Figure 11-1A). A production of pain in the calf that is brought upon by the passive stretch of the foot into a dorsiflexed position is a positive sign for thrombophlebitis. Pain may also be elicited upon palpation of the calf in conjunction with the passive stretch (Figure 11-1B).

With the knee of the involved side fully extended, the examiner pas-sively dorsiflexes the subject's foot (Figure 11-1A).

units.title: Anterior Drawer Test
units.summary: The subject is seated on a table with the knee flexed to 90 degrees and the involved foot relaxed in slight plantar flexion. The examiner sta-bilizes the tibia and fibula with one hand and grasps the calcaneus with the other (Figure 11-2A). This may also be performed with the subject in a prone position (Figure 11-2B). While assuring stabilization of the distal tibia and fibula, the exam-iner applies an anterior force to the calcaneus and talus.

This may also be performed with the subject in a prone position (Figure 11-2B).
While assuring stabilization of the distal tibia and fibula, the exam-iner applies an anterior force to the calcaneus and talus.

units.title: Talar Tilt Test (Inversion)
units.summary: The subject lies on the uninvolved side on a table with the involved foot relaxed and the knee flexed to 90 degrees. The examiner stabilizes the distal tibia with one hand while grasping the talus with the other. The examiner first places the foot in the anatomical position (neutral plantar flexion and dorsiflexion). The examiner then tilts the talus into an adducted position (Figure 11-3).
summary_sentences: The subject lies on the uninvolved side on a table with the involved foot relaxed and the knee flexed to 90 degrees.

units.title: Talar Tilt Test (Eversion)
units.summary: The subject lies on the involved side on a table with the involved foot relaxed and the knee flexed to 90 degrees. The examiner stabilizes the distal tibia with one hand while grasping the talus with the other. The examiner first places the foot in the anatomical position (neutral plantar flexion and dorsiflexion). The examiner then tilts the talus into an abducted position (Figure 11-4).

units.title: Thompson Test
units.summary: The subject lies prone on a table with the heels placed over the edge of the table. With the gastrocnemius-soleus complex relaxed, the examiner squeezes the belly of these muscles (Figure 11-5). When squeezing the calf muscles, a normal response would be to have the foot plantar flex. Therefore, an absence of plantar flexion upon squeezing would be a positive test, indicating a possible rupture of the Achilles’ tendon.

units.title: Tap or Percussion Test
units.summary: The subject lies supine with the affected leg extended and the ankle/foot just off the examining table. The examiner stands at the end of the table next to the subject's foot. The examiner positions the subject's ankle into a maximal dorsiflex-ion to optimize joint congruency and applies a firm tap to the bottom of the subject's heel (Figure 11-6). Pain at the site of injury is indicative of a fracture.

units.title: Feiss Line
units.summary: The subject sits on the examining table with the involved leg extend-ed. The examiner places a mark at the tip of the medial malleolus and at the base of the first metatarsophalangeal joint. A line is then drawn between the two points and the examiner notes the position of the nav-icular tuberosity (Figure 11-7A). The subject is asked to stand with feet 3 to 6 inches apart.

units.title: Interdigital Neuroma Test
units.summary: The subject sits on the examining table with the involved leg extend-ed. The examiner stands next to the involved foot and places one hand around the metatarsal heads (Figure 11-8). The examiner squeezes the subject's metatarsal heads together and holds for 1 to 2 minutes. Pain, tingling, or numbness in the foot, toes, or ankle is indicative of an interdigital neuroma.

units.title: Compression Test
units.summary: The subject lies supine with the affected leg extended and the ankle/foot just off the examining table. The examiner stands next to the subject's leg and notes where the pain originates. The examiner squeezes the tibia and fibula together at some point away from the painful area (Figure 11-9). Pain at the site of injury may be indicative of a fracture.

units.title: Long Bone Compression Test
units.summary: The subject sits with the affected leg extended and the foot off the end of the examining table. The examiner stands at the end of the table near the subject's foot. The examiner applies compression along the long axis of the bone of the toe or metatarsal being tested (Figure 11-10). Pain at the site of injury is indicative of a fracture.

units.title: Swing Test
units.summary: The subject should sit with the feet over the edge of the table. The examiner stands in front of the subject and places both hands over the dorsum of the subject's feet to keep them parallel to the floor. The examiner palpates the anterior aspect of the subject's talus with the thumbs (Figure 11-11A). Passively plantar flex and dorsiflex the ankle and observe the level of movement, especially with dorsiflexion (Figure 11-11B).

units.title: Kleiger's Test
units.summary: The subject sits with the leg off of the table and the knee at 90 degrees of flexion. The examiner stabilizes the distal tibia and fibula with one hand and the medial and inferior aspects of the calcaneus with the other hand. The ankle should be in a neutrally aligned position (Figure 11-12A). The examiner applies an externally rotated force upon the calcaneus.

units.title: Tinel's Sign
units.summary: The subject typically lies supine. The examiner uses his finger to tap over the medial aspect of the ankle where the posterior tibial nerve is most superficial (Figure 11-13). Pain or tingling that radiates along the pathway of the posterior tib-ial nerve is indicative of potential tarsal tunnel syndrome. Compression of the posterior tibial nerve in the tarsal tunnel will result in referred symptoms to the medial and plantar regions of the foot.

units.title: Impingement Reduction Test
units.summary: The subject is seated or standing with the arm at rest and the shoul-der internally rotated (Figure 12-1A). The examiner passively forward flexes the involved arm while main-taining shoulder internal rotation (Figure 12-1B). This motion is then repeated while the examiner applies an inferior glide to the humeral head (Figure 12-1C). The reporting of shoulder joint pain is indicative of a positive test.

units.title: Walking Arm Stress (WAS) Test
units.summary: The subject lies relaxed and supine on the examination table with arms at side (Figure 12-2A). The examiner stands at the head of the examination table and places the palm of each hand under each of the subject's scapulae (Figure 12- 2B). The subject is asked to extend one of the arms into the table force-fully while the examiner simultaneously assesses the amount of pressure felt under the scapulae. The test is repeated with the other arm.

units.title: Finger Extension Test
units.summary: The subject is seated with the hand in a resting position. The examiner first attempts to passively extend the involved distal interphalangeal (DIP) or proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joint into full extension (Figure 12-3A). The examiner then asks the subject to gently attempt to actively extend the involved DIP or PIP joint against mini-mal resistance provided by the examiner. Inability to actively or passively extend the involved DIP or PIP joint is considered to be a positive test.

units.title: Flexor Pronator Syndrome Test

The examiner attempts to "shake hands" with the subject. The sub-ject is then asked to pronate the forearm (Figure 12-4B). Pain and/or muscle weakness is considered to be a positive sign fora flexor pronator musculotendinous injury.

While assuring stabilization of the subtalar joint, the examiner applies a medial rotatory force (Figure 12-5B) and a lateral rotatory force (Figure 12-5C) through the midfoot.

units.title: Temporomandibular
units.summary: The subject can either sit or stand. The examiner taps over the masseter muscle and parotid gland (Figure 1-1). Twitching of the facial muscles, especially the masseter, indicates positive findings for facial nerve pathology. Twitching of the facial muscles may also be a result of low calcium levels in the blood.

units.title: Cervical Spine
units.summary: The subject lies supine, and the examiner sits with both hands sup-porting the subject's head. Slowly extend, rotate, and laterally flex the subject's cervical spine to each side. Then observe the subject for dizziness, blurred vision, nys-tagmus, slurred speech, or loss of consciousness (Figure 2-1). Each posi-tion should be held for approximately 30 seconds.

The examiner resists the subject's attempts to actively forward elevate both shoulders. Involvement of the supraspinatus muscle and/or tendon is suspected with noted weakness and/or a report of pain. Weakness of the supraspinatus muscle may be a result of suprascapu-lar nerve involvement.

units.title: Thoracic Spine

units.title: Lumbar Spine
units.summary: The examiner stands next to the subject. The examiner asks the subject to take a deep breath and hold while bearing down, as if having a bowel movement. Increased pain due to increased intrathecal pressure, which may be secondary to a space-occupying lesion, herniated disk, tumor, or osteo-phyte in the cervical canal is a positive finding. Pain may be localized or referred to the corresponding dermatome.

Pain may be localized or referred to the corresponding dermatome.

units.title: Sacral Spine
units.summary: The subject stands with the sacroiliac joint exposed. The examiner stands behind the subject with the thumbs over the posterior superior iliac spines (Figure 8-1A). The examiner may then leave the one thumb over the sacral spinous process and move the other thumb to the ischial tuberosity. The examiner should note whether the posterior superior iliac spines are level.

units.title: Hip
units.summary: The examiner stands on the involved side and passively flexes and adducts the subject's hip. The subject's knee is also placed in full flexion (Figure 9-1A). The examiner applies downward pressure along the shaft of the femur while simultaneously adducting and externally rotating the hip (Figure 9-1B). The examiner then adducts and internally rotates the hip while maintaining downward pressure (Figure 9-1C).

units.title: Knee
units.summary: The subject lies supine on a table. The examiner measures the distance between the superior pole of the patella to the inferior pole of the patella. The examiner next measures the distance between the inferior pole of the patella and the tibial tuber-cle (Figures 10-1A and 10-1B). A ratio is taken between the first and second measurements.

units.title: Ankle and Foot
units.summary: The subject lies supine on a table. With the knee of the involved side fully extended, the examiner pas-sively dorsiflexes the subject's foot (Figure 11-1A). A production of pain in the calf that is brought upon by the passive stretch of the foot into a dorsiflexed position is a positive sign for thrombophlebitis. Pain may also be elicited upon palpation of the calf in conjunction with the passive stretch (Figure 11-1B).

units.title: Contemporary Special Tests
units.summary: The subject is seated or standing with the arm at rest and the shoul-der internally rotated (Figure 12-1A). The examiner passively forward flexes the involved arm while main-taining shoulder internal rotation (Figure 12-1B). This motion is then repeated while the examiner applies an inferior glide to the humeral head (Figure 12-1C). The reporting of shoulder joint pain is indicative of a positive test.

units.title: Special Tests for Orthopedic Examination
units.summary: The subject can either sit or stand. The examiner taps over the masseter muscle and parotid gland (Figure 1-1). Twitching of the facial muscles, especially the masseter, indicates positive findings for facial nerve pathology. Twitching of the facial muscles may also be a result of low calcium levels in the blood. The subject lies supine, and the examiner sits with both hands sup-porting the subject's head.
